(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, at the outset I may be allowed to refer shortly to the address delivered the other evening by the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville (Mr. Lanc-tot). There is often wafted over, to us from the opposite side of the House bitter criticism of the campaign made by Nationalists in 1910-11. Apparently our Liberal friends have lost sight of the Nationalists that are found in their own ranks, among them the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville. The other evening he outstepped any Nationalist who has taken part in our campaign. I even felt .sorry that, in the midst of our present difficulties, a pronouncement of such a nature should come from a French-Canadian. Mr. Bourassa himself, although denied by his friends, has certainly never expressed himself in such terms either in his public utterances or his writings.
If excommunication there be for Mr. Bourassa, the hon. member for Laprairie should also be read out of his party.
The hon. member criticised the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Patenaude) for not having restrained his nationalist feelings and followed the dictates of his conscience in accepting a portfolio. Well, I cannot bring myself to see the crime which has been perpetrated by the man in accepting a place in the Cabinet. In a masterly effort he explained his position, and accounted for his having had to modify somewhat his viewpoint. As a matter of fact, he who insists in circumstances such as the present in sticking to his old opinions is' not a true Canadian.	*
The hon. member for Laprairie, speaking on trade and commerce, had another complaint to air. The farmers of his constituency could not dispose of their hay, or at least could not dispose of it at the price they expected. My idea is that the farmers in his county and the hon. member himself, expect too much when they ask twenty dollars a ton, or rather nineteen, with a profit of one dollar for the hon. gentleman from Laprairie. In Rimouski, we have no fault

to find, and yet our hay sells for only fifteen and sixteen dollars a ton. We are quite satisfied to sell it at that price. If the farmers of Laprairie get twenty dollars, they have no reason to complain.
Then, the hon. member thought himself bound to criticise the Government embargo on the export of hay to the United States. My idea is that the object is to prevent Americans from buying Canadian hay which they could then sell at a profit in Great Britain. The Government intended that such profit should remain with the Canadian farmers.

(Translation.) Surely the hon. member is aware that the hay which is being sold in the United States at twenty dollars a ton cannot at the present time be exported to England. The freight charges are three times the price of the hay. At the present time, you cannot ship to England under one hundred and eighty shillings a ton. The drift of my remarks was that since we were prevented by the embargo from exporting our hay to the United States, it was unfair for the Government to import American hay, in competition with ours, to have that hay re-pressed at Montreal and exported to England. Do you think it fair, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers of Canada should have to compete with this American hay?
Order, order.

(Translation.) In any
case, even after the explanations of the hon. member I agree with the reasons given by the hon. the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell) in his explanation of the embargo placed upon the export of hay to the States the purpose of which he said, was to keep in Canada a quantity of hay sufficient for the army.
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I insist on my hon. friend not attributing to me statements I have not made. I have not criticised the Government for placing an embargo on the export of hay.
(Translation.) The hon. member for Rimouski has the floor and I should request the hon. member for Laprairie not to interrupt.

Mr. Speaker, I am
through with what remarks I wished to make on the speech of the hon. member for Laprairie, and I shall now pass to a consideration of the Budget.
My first care will be to congratulate the hon. the Minister of Finance on his clear

and definite statement of the country's financial situation, as set out in his speech on the Budget. In a masterly manner, he has traced out his policy and the means to be taken to meet the present crisis. The hon. the Minister of Finance is a valuable acquisition. Lie certainly is the man for the position. No one better qualified could be found at the present time to fill the most difficult position of Dominion tax-collector and work out a satisfactory solution of the present economical problem. It is given to nations in critical! times to find among its citizens men capable of coping with great events.
To what has already been said by previous distinguished speakers, I feel I may subjoin my own remarks.
The House has just been told that the long drawn-out investigation on the high cost of living is completed. I am no expert in economics; yet, whatever be the conclusions the commissioners have arrived at, I find it my duty to say that two of the most potent factors in the increase of the cost of living are:-	[DOT]
1.	The excessive immigration of Jews and labourers from other countries;
2.	The lack of farmers and the exodus from country to city.
The Jewish immigration is a real plague. I am told that Montreal alone accounts for 50,000.

And they
are good citizens.

No doubt; they likely are electors of my hon. friend; 76,681 of them in Canada, without taking into account those who are disseminated throughout the country. Out of all that number I should welcome any one who would name a single Jew who settled on the land with the intention of improving it. Not one came to Canada with that purpose in mind. On the contrary, every where they are found as dealers, pedlars, real estate agents, etc., not one is of any benefit to Canada. The other day it was said in my hearing in this House that after the war a strong influx would set in. Should that be the case, I should impress upon the Government and upon the Immigration authorities the necessity of barring from Canada not only those who would come here to reside without a family, but also any man who would comes without the avowed purpose of tilling the land.
We have no place for a single foreign labourer; farmers are those we want. We have no further need of foreigners as real estate agents, dealers, shopkeepers, and what not. If it be intended to lower the

cost of living, let us cut out idle people, who live on other people's labour, and let us increase the number of our farmers. The Government should pass some enactment empowering it to deport any person coming into this country who will not settle on a farm. Not only should it be required that an immigrant be the head of a family and undertake to become a farmer, but our agents should keep trace of him to see that he lives up to his obligations.
An energetic move should also be made to induce our farmers' sons to follow their father's noble calling in the great profession of soil and stock husbandry.
I must say that the two hundred and fifty million dollar Budget submitted us this year appears to me quite heavy for the country, although our friends on the other side are prepared to endorse every item. I shall insist on what I said last year in this respect. The countries at war, Great Britain in particular, should see to the maintenance of our soldiers as soon as they leave Canadian soil and all expenditure for munitions and the maintenance of our troops across the ocean should not be borne by us.
I further claim that there is no valid reason why our forces should be raised to
500.000	troops when we have only 60,000 to
70.000	at the front. It is a wise policy 'to train soldiers in advance, but 'why undergo ' excessive expenditure, when our first contingent was trained in five or six months and gave such a good account of itself on the battlefield that it east glory and pride on the Canadian name. My opinion is that we have too many soldiers in training, taking all the place on the railway trains. The reply will be made that we must prepare for every possible contingency. However, I should prefer on the part of the Government a little more foresight here at home. It seems to me that certain individuals who . apparently are acting the part of spies are allowed too much freedom. I inquired lately as to the number of Germans in the Civil Service and on my expressing astonishment at their being kept in employment, the answer was that:
As they fulfil the duties of their position conscientiously, the Government sees no reason why it should dispense with their services.
To my mind, such an explanation will no more satisfy the country than it does me. What a mere certificate of naturalization, the signing of a mere scrap of paper which Germany tears into shreds, and of the kind she has already thrown to the four winds of Heaven, will be sufficient to bind a citizen of the Kaiser and turn him into a
citizen of his adoptive country in time of war! Let us have some sense. Will that certificate of naturalization, without more, change the colour of the blood that flows in the veins of a German or an Austrian? Belgium stands as an example and the international laws trampled under are a clear proof of the stock we should place in a German's signature.
The length of time one resides in Canada does not count for anything when feelings have to be stifled and a man's origin to be eradicated from his memory. I myself am a case in point. In 1632, almost three hundred years ago, my first ancestor settled in this country; we are loyal to our institutions and true to our word; but still we retain our love for our old Mother France. We have wept over its political wrongdoings, but the soil remains the soil of our forefathers and the object of our deep affection, and in a war between England and France, on what side would be found my sympathies? On the side of France. Why should a German be different from any other human being?
Study the past, and you will be readily convinced that I am right, a hundred times right. It is not fair that the Government should keep in its service a single citizen of German origin. Without proof that they are disloyal subjects, we have at least reason to be suspicious of them, whatever the number of years they have resided in this country.
At any rate we have had a striking example only recently, of their way of looking at things, in the case of the notorious Lincoln, a fugitive from English justice, who has just been arrested by the New York police. That clever German had come to reside in England a number of years ago. He was naturalized and then was elected to the House of Commons at Westminster, where he sat during one or two parliaments. As soon as war was declared, he hurried across the Atlantic and did not deem it in anyway shameful to say openly that he had acted the part of a spy.
Let me be allowed at this juncture a short digression. I shall first quote from the speech of the brave Colonel Currie, member for Simcoe:
Our ideas of the French people are in many cases entirely erroneous. The ideas put in books by novelists are often contemptible. There are no finer people, no more casual people, no more cool and collected people under danger-and I have seen them in the fight, in the middle of it-than the French.
These few words pronounced in sincere language by a man who has risked his life on the battlefields of Europe, by a man that

we know to have fulfilled his duty as a soldier and a brave man, who saw so many other brave men falling alongside of him, and to whom death was despised, have made me cry. Why so ? Because I then thought of our own French-Can-adians, descendants of that glorious race referred to by Colonel Currie, to-day victims of uncalled for, senseless and shameful tyranny. We, priding ourselves on our descent from those heroes who know when to die for their country, we also are determined to the last man to do our duty and prove to the world that we are ready to make the sacrifice of our lives when circumstances require. But what stands in our way? The ban which has been placed on our language in almost every province of this Confederation, the treatment meted us by the majority in this country. We whose ancestors have opened the continent to the cross and to civilization; we, whose missionaries have suffered martyrdom at the hands of the heathen on Canadian soil; we, who have been in possession of this soil for over three hundred years, we are treated as trespassers, as Germans and Indians? Why? Because we have remained true to the language of our forefathers.
,We are not understood by our English speaking countrymen; we occupy of right the little bit of land we hold of the creator, the little bit of land we want to cultivate, on which it is our wish to live, respectful of our country's laws; to live in peace, speaking the language of our ancestors, of those same Frenchmen who know so well how to fight and die.
We are prevented from enlisting before we ever attempt to do so; we are deprived of our full share on the death-roll, by the persecution we are undergoing in our schools. We are asked in the face of the treatment we receive to take our place in the ranks of those glorious soldiers who are going to die for their country! It passes all comprehension.
The reproach is cast to us, especially in the Ontario newspapers, that we are not enlisting as we should. I will not admit that such is the case, but the saying is current. Yet after the war, when the count is made, it will be found that the number of Frenchspeaking and English-speaking recruits of Canadian origin will have been about equal and that the proportion of French-Oanadians from now on will have greatly increased. Even at this date, there are many French-Canadian units in English-speaking regiments, and officers have told me that many Frenchmen have enlisted in English regi-

ments, some of whom are even now at Belleville and reckoned among English speaking recruits.
Notwithstanding our grievances, I should like to see recruiting still more active. Yet my county of Rimouski has already given more than two hundred recruits, a fair number of whom are now at the front, and four of whom have already fallen on the firing line. I have no hestitation in stating that if the persecution against French was called off, and that language allowed to be taught untrammelled, a thousand soldiers could easily be enlisted in the county of Rimouski alone, and that in a very short time. The same thing would happen throughout the whole of Quebec. All the harangues of Bourassa and Lavergne could not impede or diminish enlistment, because at this date not two per cent of the population agree with them.

(Translation.) Things
have much changed.
Mr. BOULAY; (Translation.) Yes, things have changed. I said so at the beginning and gave the explanation. In 1896, you also did change. It has been said that whoever never changes his views is a fool.
We have no wish to prevent the Englishspeaking majority from using their language, we are still more loath to impose ours on them; on the contrary, we want our own children to learn the two languages that are official in this country. Such is our ambition, and a legitimate one indeed. The same ambition is to be found at all periods and among all nations. Why not so with the French who inhabit Canada? We have not degenerated. The qualities that characterize the French of France are to be found in the French of Canada. We have one desire at heart, freedom, yes, that freedom which allows the child in the cradle to breathe freedom which makes one give his life in the defence of his country, of his motherland.
I shall now speak on a subject touched upon by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). He claimed that we should cut short all expenditure for public works, which are not strictly necessary. He insisted particularly on the Hudson Bay railway. It does seem to me that if there is an item of expenditure which should be cut off, it is indeed the construction of the Hudson Bay railway and all works connected with it. As a matter of fact, I never could understand why that construction was undertaken. Is it for the purpose of giving the western grain an earlier outlet?

But we have already three railways that can accommodate three such harvests like this year's, which however is quite abundant. How can it be said as a plausible justification that the purpose is to afford early shipping to western wheat, since, at the time wheat is ready for shipping, navigation has been closed for a long while already, and so, not before the following mid-summer, could the Hudson Bay road be utilized.
Are the millions of dollars now to be expended intended to satisfy the numerous requests made to the Liberal Government and which this Government has promised to grant? There was no obligation on our part to carry out the promises of the late administration. Even the present expenditure fails to satisfy the western farmers. Their representatives in this House show dissatisfaction. They dare not criticise the construction of that railway, but they take hours, days and even weeks of our precious [DOT] time in pressing for the free export of wheat to the American markets. Free wheat is their shibboleth. If their sole ambition is to reach the American markets, why build a new railway at great expense to give a better outlet to their wheat? If our western countrymen cannot be satisfied with the expenditure of millions and millions for their sole benefit, let us do away with those enormous expenses, at least during the war. Let us put a stop to the gigantic building operations on the Hudson Bay railway, and we shall have done something to the country's advantage.
Let us also postpone the work in St. John harbour and the dredging of Courtenay bay. We have a splendid winter harbour at Halifax; why go on with those immense works at St. John? A small trip to Courtenay bay will convince you that we are wasting millions in digging a mud channel. Some justification could at least be found if a shorter route were made for ocean vessels, but on the contrary the ocean voyage by vessels running into St. John is increased by two hundred miles.
I quite understand that the Liberal party and the present Government in turn strive to construct as many public works as possible, and spend as much as possible at St. John. The city of St. John is represented in this House and has always been by Cabinet Ministers, but it behooves the rest of the country to approve or disapprove of all this expenditure.
The hon. member for St. John, I presume, place above the special interest of their city the general interest of the country. To hear
them in this House, they have nothing at heart so much as the welfare of Canada.
I believe that the enormous expenditure in the misty harbour of St. John is a direct cause of the delay in bringing about the winter navigation of the St. Lawrence.
I believe previous experience has shown that ocean liners could with safety sail up to Rimouski or to the Saguenay and even to Quebec during the whole of December every year.
Yet that project of winter navigation has been relegated to the back ground to satisfy the ambitions of our two Atlantic ports, quite legitimate in the case of Halifax harbour, but unfair in the case of St. John.
I shall then conclude with the remark that the real interests of the country require that the works in St. John harbour and Courtenay bay and on the Hudson Bay line be stopped ; that there ought to be enlisted only the number of soldiers strictly required and that steps should be taken to regulate the immigration which will flow into Canada after the war.

The debate on the Budget offers many advantages to members of this House, because we are at liberty to discuss during it many important subjects; in fact, almost any subject. It is not my intention to follow my hon. friend (Mr. Boulay) in all that he has said, because only one or two of his remarks call for a reply. At the outset of his remarks, when he was discussing the question of immigration, he condemned a certain element of our citizens, good, law-abiding people, declaring that they should be refused admission to Canada. He referred in this way to the Hebrews, the Jewish people, in this country. I do not believe it is fair for any member to criticise any citizen of Canada in this way; we have always said that we were a democratic country, that our doors were wide open for good, law-abiding citizens, and it is especially unfair to speak in this way of the Jews, because they are a class of people who will become naturalized as quickly as the laws of the land in which they settle will permit.
Hear, hear.

I belong to a class of people who do not believe in any line of either creed, colour or nationality, and if I am to take the words of the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) the other night when he was speaking with reference to conditions at the front, we must believe, in fact he has proved to us, that there were

no questions of nationality, creed or colour among the men on the firing line. So I do not believe it becomes the hon. member for Rimouski to try to throw any slur upon these people as he did when he plainly stated in French that the Jews in this country were a plague. I take issue with this statement. I have no special mission to defend the Jewish people any more than any one else, but as the representative of a city where there are a number of Jewish inhabitants, I say it is unfair, unjust, and uncalled-for for any member of the House to use such language. Towards the close of his remarks my hon. friend reproached the city of St. John for always having the advantage of having a minister of the Crown to represent it. If any one in this House should say nothing on this line, it is surely the hon. member for Rimouski himself. Perhaps at present he has nobody in his family whom he would like to place in any of the departments of the Government; but if I were to take the list of his friends and relations whom he has placed in the different departments and place it before the hon. member, surely he would not attack the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) nor the ex-Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley), the other representative of that city, to-day.
We have heard in this House, particularly yesterday and a few days before, a full discussion of the wheat question. No family in this or any other country can do without the staple of life, bread. This is a very acute question, not only in the cities but everywhere. The report of the Royal Commission on the High Cost of Living was placed in the hands of the members of the House within the last few days, and, in the short time at my disposal since I have devoted a good deal of attention to its contents. The report undoubtedly contains a great number of statistics, but outside of that I do not like to say much about it. In going through this report, 1 wondered why, even yesterday, during that famous discussion, the Solicitor General, who showed such great sympathy for minorities, yet would not favour the motion that was before the House.
While on the question of minorities, may I say a few words with reference to another question of importance? From what I have heard lately I am tempted to ask if what is transpiring in the city of Ottawa and in this province is not the result of a system

of German espionage established to prevent recruiting in the province of Quebec. I

really believe that even Bernsdorf could not have done better, if he had been trying to stir nationality against nationality, than the system now in operation in the province of Ontario. I just cite that in passing, because I am going to ask members of this House, although the subject is outside of our jurisdiction, to use their good offices to terminate the dissention that now exists. We preach every day patriotism, and patriotism, and always patriotism. I may not understand patriotism as well as some other members, but surely in patriotism there is no question of nationality, or creed, or colour. It seems to me that the members of this House should do all in their power and use their good offices in that respect.
Reverting to the bread question, I wish to place on Hansard some figures showing a comparison between the prices of bread in the different parts of the world. These figures are found in volume 1, at pages 74T and 748, and cover Chicago, Montreal, Liverpool and London. That seems a fair comparison. The report is for the year 1909. One might say that there has been quite a change since, but nevertheless we have to take the report as it is given. We find that from a barrel of flour weighing 196 pounds a bakerican make 280 pounds of bread. We find also that the total cost of everything that he adds to that barrel of flour to make that 280 pounds is $1.13. In Chicago, where the wages received by workingmen are between 20 and 22j per cent higher than in Montreal, 280 . pounds of bread cost $12.76, while in Montreal, for the same quantity, the price was $14.56; in Toronto $11.20, and in Ottawa $12.54; in Liverpool, England, $6.94, and in London $7.61. It sold in Montreal, for twice the price that was charged in Liverpool or London. So much has been said with respect to the price of flour that I desire to quote prices given in this same report, at page 754, in a report from Mr. W. A. Black, managing director of the Ogilvie Milling Company. He gives the figures in criticising some other figures that appear in the paper as showing the difference in the price of flour in different places. He states that the top grade of flour costs in Winnipeg $4.50 and in London $4.18, a difference of 32 cents; patents, $4.80 in Winnipeg, $4.06 in London; bakers, $4 in Winnipeg, $3.60 in London. We can see by these figures, given by this managing director himself, that flour sold cheaper in London than in Winnipeg, and also that bread cost in London not much more than half what it

cost in Montreal. There is something radically wrong somewhere. I have said in this House in previous years that the bread trust organized in Toronto a few years ago was exceedingly powerful, and in that statement I made no mistake. They have spread everywhere. They have extended their operations to Montreal, and the profits which they are making are evidently enormous. It is a question whether these institutions will be covered by the taxation proposals of the Minister of Finance. That will depend largely on the amount of watered stock they have.

They will not pay
anything.

My hon. friend tells me they will not pay anything; T take his word for it. If I am to take my hon. friend's statement that these companies are not going to pay any taxes, is it advisable that we should any longer permit companies of this kind to exploit the masses of our people? It is impossible at the present time for any family to do without bread; there is no family poor enough or small enough to get along without the staple of life, that is, bread, and as I have stated it is a very acute question in our city. I go directly to the root of the whole question. If we could get the wheat cheaper we could compel the millers to sell the flour a little cheaper, and then we would have a basis on which to go to .tire baker -and say to him: "You cannot complain about the high cost of flour, because you. are now paying a lower price for it." According to the same report, at page 137 of the first volume, there is a statement	by	the Department of
Labour of what is necessary for a family to live for a whole week, based on an income of $800 during the year.' According to their report, a family of five would eat fifteen pounds of bread per week. You can imagine what that means, always keeping in mind the hundred per cent difference between London and Montreal. When I take the report brought down by the Department of Labour, previous to the report of the High Cost of Living Commission, although the former is included in the latter, I notice that the writer of the report fixes $800 as the amount that it will cost a family of five to live for a year, but he has forgotten a great many things, and - amongst them some of the most important things of life. For instance, he has forgotten sickness, church contributions, the carfare that the workingman must pay to reach his place of employment, furniture, linen, etc. According to the figures contained in this report, $160 would not be any too much to add for these items, and we would reach $1,123 if we were to add all the absolute necessaries of life omitted from the list contained in the report. Every time that a workingman buys something-I do not care what it is-he pays the equivalent of the tariff rate on that article. The tariff tax is applied to every dollar's worth that he purchases. Not only on goods that are imported into this country does he pay the tax, but he pays it on the goods that are Manufactured in the country. You know as well as I do that the tariff is the basis of the prices charged for goods manufactured in Canada. You cannot buy a pin, or anything else, but the tariff will set the price of it. If I take a rate of thirty per cent as representing the rate of tariff taxation, the workingman will have to pay thirty per [DOT]cent additional on every dollar's worth that he purchases during the year.
I have a few figures here which I want to place on Hansard, and which I want to present to the members of this House, showing that we pay far more in taxation than we realize on the goods which we purchase, of which taxation the Government only receive a certain portion under the system now in operation. Taking the population of Canad,a at 7,500,000, and dividing this number by five, you get the number of families as 1,500,000. According to the report of the Department of Labour, it costs $800 per family to live, and on that basis you have $1,200,000,000 as the annual expenditure of these 1,500,000 families in the country. I know that I am far below the truth when I accept the estimate of $800 per family. If you add 30 per cent to that, which means that for every dollar we spend we pay 30 cents additional 'indirectly, you will find that this indirect taxation amounts to $360,000,000 every year. We take no less than $360,000,000 every year from the pockets of the consumers, the poorer classes especially, in taxation. According to the blue-book, 21 per cent is the maximum amount that the Government receive from the tariff, and I doubt very much if they receive that much.
Now, I would like to show by way of illustration the effect of the 7^ per cent duty which was added to the tax on raw material last year. What does it mean? Let us take a value of $100, by way of example, and see what it amounts to with the per cent added. One hundred dollars

worth of raw -material, when it is landed in the factory, is, with the duty added, worth $107.50. I am not speaking of the profit of the person who furnishes the raw material. If you add 25 per cent, which is nothing but fair, for the profit and overhead charges of the manufacturer, you find that the article costs the wholesale house $134.37. The wholesale -man also must make a profit of 25 per cent. When it Teaches the retailer it is worth $177.96. Is it unfair to expect that the retailer -should also make 25 per cent profit? They say that 221 per cent is the minimum amount that a business -man can allow for overhead charges. We therefore add 25 per cent as' the retailer's profit, and when the article reaches the consumer its cost has increased to $222.45. The. article -starts out with a value of $107.50, and by the time it reaches the consumer it has attained a price of $222.45 as a^result .of our present system. I do not want to take the rate of 30 per cent, because I -am afraid that some -members in the House might -say that it was too high.
1-t is because of thi-s excessive burden of indirect taxation that I have always said, every time I have had an opportunity of discussing this subject, that I was in favour of another system of taxation. I do not care whether the Minister of -Finance wants to adopt a new system now or not, he will be compelled by the logic of events to change it. I am not opposed to a system of direct taxation, because I want to see taxes .imposed in such a form as to make an equitable distribution of the burden amongst all. Under the system proposed by the Minister of Finance there are many institutions now in existence which will not -contribute a cent of the taxes* What about the high-salaried men? There are many men in this country who are receiving $10,000, $15,000, $25,000 a year. I know of one who works for the Government who is receiving $20,000 a year, and he goes scot free. There are many others in a similar position. I do not think it is fair. That is why I am in favour of a change in the present system of taxation. If my hon. friend the Minister of Finance would come before this House with a direct system of taxation I would favour it. I do not believe there is any other equitable way unless you are going to tax the land- itself. Suppose' you, Mr. Speaker, purchase a lot for a thousand dollars and build a house upon it. There are two or three vacant lots adjoining your property. Your neighbour

also builds a house and you both put a certain amount of money into your improvements. You wish to make your property attractive in appearance and you make a garden and improve your grounds. A man comes along and buys one of the vacant lots for perhaps $1,000, and, as a result of the improvements which you and your neighbour have put upon your properties, this vacant lot, in two or three years, attains a value of perhaps $5,000. The purchaser of this vacant land has had nothing to do with bringing about this increased value, it being the result simply of the improvement of the surrounding property. Then, if you paint your house, plant shade trees about it and cultivate a garden, thus adding to the attractive appearance of your property, the chances are that an addition of $200 or $300 will be made to your assessment, and your taxation will be increased.
When anybody proposes a system of direct taxation, or of land taxation, the cry goes up that it is too radical. We .are always afraid of radical things here, but in two or three years what are supposed to be radical systems are accepted as commonplace, natural, and obvious. If we cannot have land taxation, let us have an income tax. Why should we not tax hon. members of this House who are receiving $2,500 a year? Why should we not tax the indemnities and salaries of ministers of the Crown? If we had an income tax of -two per cent we could collect in the city of Ottawa alone $175,000 a year from the high-salaried civil servants. I am willing to pay my share if other hon. gentlemen are.
The present, system of taxation imposes a heavy burden on the poorest class in this country. The ba-sis of the cost of living in any country is the tariff. Suppose, for instance, that the labour men of this country succeeded after a long -struggle in raising wages by twenty-five cents a day; -the Government could wipe out -that increase in a moment by simply raising the tariff on the goods -the workmen consume. The moment the tariff goes up, the cost of living increases. Will any one in this House say -that salaries have not decreased during the last two years ot that the cost of living has decreased? According to the report laid on the table a few days ago, the cost of living has increased by five per cent, and wages have decreased-not in the shell industry, of course. We have recent proof that wages are decreasing in this country in the telegram I read to the House a few

minutes ago to the effect that Vickers-Maxim want to Teduoe by 2J cents an hour the pay of their labourers; and that is a firm that is getting big money on its contracts.
Let us look for a moment at the system of taxation in Wisconsin. Speaking from memory, I believe that every bachelor in that state earning over $800 a year is taxed. Why should we not have a similar tax here? Wisconsin also taxes the married man who earns over $1,500 a year, after making an allowance of $200 for each child he has. Hon. gentlemen might retort that these taxes would not yield much money in the province of Quebec. Perhaps so. I am sure that in a great many places in my province very little money would be collected by taxes of that kind. It is only fair that bachelors should be taxed. A bachelor earning $800 a year is better off than a married man earning $1,500. What expenses has a bachelor got? Sometimes he pays his board, and sometimes he jumps it; he has nobody to carry with him when he goes. The Finance Minister saw difficulties in the way of collecting an income tax, but I think it could be very easily collected in the same way that we collect customs duties. The income tax has been very successful in the United States, where $83,000,000 was raised by it the first year. When there was talk of imposing the tax there, all the high-salaried people ran down to Washington and did all they could to prevent the imposition of the tax. But we don't hear any complaints about it to-day; they have made up their minds that it is only fair that they should be taxed.
I -hope that before the Finance Minister brings down his Bill he will give serious thought to the suggestions I have made. I am convinced that this taxation is going to fall most heavily on the poor people of this country; I am positive of that. I hope no one will say that the poorer classes of this country have not done their share as regards recruiting. As soon as the question of recruiting came up amongst the organized labour men of this country, we in quired from headquarters, which are not in this country, what our attitude should be, and they said that as long as the men were fighting at the front they would pay their sick benefit, and that if they got killed they would pay their insurance benefit. It seems to me that the labour men of this country are doing their share in- this war. I told the Finance Minister last year that the taxation he was
then imposing would fall most heavily upon the poor people of this country, and so it has proved. A poor man cannot buy a box of pills' from a drug store without paying from two to five cents war tax. It was said last year that the tax would be paid, not by the consumer, but by the druggist, either wholesaler or retailer. The fact is the consumer pays the tax in every instance.
I should like to say a few word,s in regard to soldiers' pensions. It has been my privilege to see quite a number of returned soldiers, for I have the honour to be a member of one of the commissions appointed to search for work for returned soldiers. I think everybody will agree that in the future we shall have to pay out a large sum for pensions, and it seems to me that we might as well make a thorough job of the entire pension system now. Why not, when we are arranging for pensions for soldiers, provide a general old-age-pension scheme? We are juggling with millions, and a few millions more or less will make no difference.
I am one of those who has declared himself in this House to be against war. I have always been opposed to war-and it might fairly be asked why I am not opposed to this present war. The reason I do not oppose Canada's participation in this war is the same that was given by the president of the American Federation of Labour at the last convention, when he said that he had changed his mind in regard to war since he had seen all the labour men of Great Britain and, France rallying round the flag to fight for civilization. It has been exactly the same with me. I have said in this House before, and I say it again now, that I am willing to vote any amount of money required to carry on the war, provided the money will be spent properly. I hope no one will accuse me for not enrolling under the fag; I am too old for that. I myself would not criticise any one for not enlisting, but I take off my hat to the soldier, and say he is a man. Labour men have done splendidly in this war. A large part of the blood that has stained, the dunes of Flanders has flowed from the veins of the labour men of this country, who have made up their minds that this is a fight for right, a fight for liberty, and the liberty that the workmen of Great Britain fought for so stoutly. When I read of the manner in which the labouring men of Great Britain had to hide themselves in

cellars to safeguard their rights, and how they had to fight for the liberty which they had so, far achieved, I made up my mind that the labour men of this-country, whenever their rights might be menaced, would do all in their power to safeguard the liberty that was so dearly bought by our British brothers.
I hope the Minister of Finance, in framing his taxes, will take into consideration those who can well afford to pay. Let him put a stop to the "get-rich-quick" idea, and change h,is system so that there will be less taxation imposed upon the poorer classes of this country.

Mr. Speaker, a few years ago, before I became a member of this House, when I learned through the press of the election of my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Ver-ville), over a Liberal nominated by a Liberal convention in that constituency, I thought it a very fortunate circumstance. It struck me as being very appropriate that the great interests of labour in this country should have in this Parliament a representative who could speak exclusively for labour.
Did my hon. friend say that I was chosen by a Liberal convention?

No, I do not think that even a Liberal convention would be guilty of that. What I said was that the hon. gentleman was elected in opposition to the nominee of a Liberal convention.
After having obtained a seat in this House and after having had an opportunity of observing the attitude of my hon. friend, I was at a loss to understand just what the distinction was between a labour representative and a hidebound Grit, and I have never yet been able to see in the attitude of my hon. friend anything that has convinced me that he has in his mind any very clear distinction between the two. I did think, however, when this Budget was brought down, that now my hon. friend would have an opportunity, if he really had at heart the interests of the great labour party, to show that he stood for the interests of labour, separate and apart from the principles of Gritism. But after hearing him to-day condemn in the most unmeasured terms this tariff which is very greatly in the interest of labour, and, furthermore, after hearing him speak so glibly about a matter of a few million dollars not amounting to anything,

I made up my mind that there was very little in common between my hon. friend and the labour party which he pretends to
represent.
1 am informed that, in times past, when the Budget was brought down, the Opposition were in the habit of immediately rising to define the attitude of their party in respect to the Budget proposals. In former times, as soon as the Minister of Finance threw down the gage of battle it was taken up; but this year-and perhaps the change has dated back one or two years-there has been a change of tactics. This year two full days were allowed to elapse, with the glove of the Minister of Finance in the lists, before the financial critic of the Opposition could make up his mind whether it was . better for him to pick up the glove or to run away. This I understand is due to a change in party tactics. In the otld days, the Opposition party was led by men having seats in this House, and members of the Opposition were enabled to lay down a policy both for themselves in this House and for their party in the country outside. That policy apparently has 'been changed just as there has been a radical change in military tactics. In former times a commander went into battle at the head of his men. To-day, I am informed, the direction of a military engagement is not in the trenches, but some general, sitting miles back in a little office with plans and despatches before him, directs the conduct of the battle. So it is in this House at the present time. Hon. gentlemen in the trenches opposite do not direct their own movements; as a matter of fact, there is an advisory committee composed largely of persons not having seats in this House, in many instances of persons who have actually been rejected by the people of this country. This committee, which is out side of this House altogether, determines when hon. gentlemen opposite shall march to the attack and when they shall retreat.
Personally, I am not in favour of such a system. It is not democratic; it is not fair to hon. gentlemen opposite, and it seems to me that an hon. gentleman who is entrusted with looking after his constituents, in whose ability his constituents have enough confidence to send him here, should be allowed to act for himself after he is elected.
Further than that, such a system tends to do away with responsibility. I believe that hon. gentlemen opposite have made many wild and reckless statements which

would never have been made had they been allowed to think these things out for themselves, had they not been dictated to by people outside. When the Opposition are not allowed to think for themselves, when they are controlled by an outside party and when they must refer everything to people outside of this House, delay is caused and the debate drags. If hon. gentlemen opposite were allowed to get together and decide for themselves their own policy, they could act with cohesion; but as it is, hon. members opposite from the Maritime Provinces look for guidance to an individual who has not a seat in this House and who resides somewhere down in Nova Scotia, and they follow him and hon. gentlemen opposite from the West look to some one residing in the West for their judgment, and the result is confusion amongst them. It is no -wonder therefore that we have found confusion and contradiction amongst the members opposite who have spoken in this debate. For instance, we have the hon. junior member for Halifax declaring that the duty on apples is a bad thing 'because the apple is a staple article of consumption, and we have the hon. member for Medioine Hat (Mr. Buchanan) objecting to the duty on the ground that apples are a luxury. Again, we have the hon. member for Halifax stating that seven per cent is not sufficient for a business interest to obtain by way of return on the investment of capital, and we have the hon. member for Medicine Hat claiming that it is too much. However, I suppose hon. gentlemen opposite will not attach much importance to my views in reference to the management of their internal affairs, and I d,o not suppose that, inasmuch as this is a domestic matter, I should say much about it. Constitutionally, we are bound to regard hon. gentlemen opposite as the authors of their own work; constitutionally we are bound to regard them as statesmen, and not megaphones. And so when the financial critic of the Opposition rises to deliver his views in reference to the Budget he binds his party in this House and out of this House for weal or for woe-and I think that in this instance it was mostly for woe.
It seems to me that the Budget presented, by tbe Minister of Finance, especially when you consider the conditions under which it was brought down, is the most encouraging and the most courageous Budget ever brought before this Parliament. A Finance Minister who could announce in one Budget the floating of loans at more favourable rates than are secured by the wealthiest countries in the world; could announce that we have overdrafts nowhere and trade balances both at home and abroad; could announce the greatest aggregate trade in the history of the country; could announce a surplus of $45,000,000 and a trade balance in our favour of $200,000,000, it seems to me is a Finance Minister who might fairly expect words of congratulation even from very much less generous people than hon. gentlemen opposite. - But no words of congratulation, no words of commendation, have fallen from the lips of hon. gentlemen opposite, so far as I have heard, certainly none from those of the hon. gentleman who prides himself on his fairness, the financial critic of the Opposition. From him we have not a word that would even savour of congratulation or commendation for the Minister of Finance.
I wish to point out that in his general public uterances there has been a marked change in that hon. gentleman (Mr. A. K. Maclean) in a few years. I have noted in his speeches on successive budgets the development of a wonderful religious spirit. There was a time, when he sat on this side, when he paid little attention to divine agencies and exalted and magnified the human. This sin clung to him even after he went over to the other side of the House. Let me quote what he said in 1912 when speaking on the Budget:
Increased imports and exports, a buoyant revenue, a great increase in our immigration and commerce are all indications to a remarkable degree of our prosperity, and I trust are the tokens of a still greater future for this young country. We upon this side of the House follow with considerable interest the successful operations of the many political programmes or policies initiated by the late Government, and I am glad to observe that the continuation of this programme or policies in the hands of hon. gentlemen opposite is evep productive of good.
You see it was the Government-it was human agency that was responsible for all these benefits, and it was only because the Government followed the practices of hon. gentlemen opposite that the sun shone and the harvests were bountiful. In the next year, in his address on the Budget, he said:
I think I shall be able to show that the Government deliberately and in the face of warning brought about our present financial condition, that they never did and are not to-day making an effort to maintain the equilibrium between revenue and expenditure and place public expenditures upon a sound basis. They are almost entirely responsible for our present financial position.



Again, the Government is responsible. But, apparently, the vicissitudes of opposition have had an effect upon him, they have melted his stony heart, broken down the middle wall of partition; and so this year, speaking on the Budget, he shows almost a Christian spirit, and says-
After the passing of almost a year hon. gentlemen opposite will agree with me that this prediction was idle, as was expected, and that any stimulation that came to Canadian industry or any relief that came to unemployment was not the result of the tariff taxation of last year, but one of the incidents of the world wide calamity, and further that any stimulation that came to Canadian agriculture was due to the efforts of men and the blessings of God, not to the tariff of the Minister of Finance.
The right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition had at one time the same weakness as my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax. He used to claim credit for the very sunshine and for bountiful harvests, and it was only in deference to the religious sentiment of this country that he finally did admit Providence 'nto partnership with himself.
On this side of the House we have never failed in that regard. This Liberal-Conservative party has always recognized its dependence on Providence. But it has always recognized also the truth of that principle that Heaven helps him who is willing to help himself. And if ever there was a Government that had fulfilled that condition precedent to divine assistance, it is this Government; if ever there was a Finance Minister who could claim credit for prosperity, it seems to me it is the present Finance Minister. A Government that, in the first place, started the campaign for greater production; a Government that gave the farmer consideration in its tariff; a Government that^ educated the farmers to produce more, and actually advanced to the farmers in the West $13,000,000 to aid them in buying seed grain -it seems to me that such a Government is in a position to claim some of the credit for the bountiful harvest which has blessed this country. This is a case of a Govern-ernment scattering plenty o'er a smiling land, and of Providence blessing, and bountifully blessing, the work of its handmaid.
I think, however, that the features of the Budget which call for particular satisfaction on the part of the people even more than the splendid indications of prosperity that it discloses, are its tax features. In the past, in this country, it has been the

poor man who has paid the taxes, and the big interests which make and break Governments have been almost exempt. That is so even in our municipalities-the small holder of property is usually taxed to the limit, while his wealthy brother escapes with very -little taxation. For the first time in the history of this country a Minister of Finance has had the courage to put forth his hand upon the great, and to tax the people who had the money to pay and who were getting something out of the country. It required courage, it required sagacity to do that; and I believe the people will give the Finance Minister great credit for what he has done. Hon. gentlemen opposite have a new found solicitude for the business interests in this country. The Liberal party in this country has never been fair to the business interests. They have always referred to them as the mergers, the trusts and the combines. They have even gone so far as to refer to them as porch climbers, and' any consideration which this Government has been able to give to the business interests in protection from their rapacious competitors in the United States, they have been able to give only at the bayonet's point, only after the most severe opposition from hon. gentlemen opposite. I say the Liberal party has not been fair with the business interests in this country, but the greatest injustice the Liberal party in this House has ever done to the business interest is to doubt its willingness at this juncture to pay these taxes. I believe that the business interests in this country realise that they get more out of this country by way of protection than the smaller earner of income, whom hon. gentlemen opposite would tax. I believe it realizes it is up to it to pay more towards the maintenance of this country than does the small income earner, and I believe the business interest will gladly do this. I believe that when the business interests consider the fact that business interests in Germany are paying fifty per cent in order to keep up a despicable and detestable tyranny in that country, they will regard it as a privilege to contribute one quarter of their earnings over seven per cent to keep up and maintain and protect the most glorious and-free institutions that the world has ever seen. The hon. member for Halifax protested that seven per cent was not enough' for a business interest to receive upon its invested capital, and he said [DOT] it was unfair to tax the overplus on seven per cent in order to maintain the institutions of this country. These words of

his bound the Liberal party, as they were uttered by the financial critic of that party, but it is no wonder that my hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Buchanan) refused to agree to them and protested his unwillingness to accept that doctrine. The hon. member for Halifax contended that this tax would discourage the investment of foreign capital in this country. I say that apy foreign investor of capital who would be unwilling to invest capital in this .	country with a prospect that he
5 p,.m. be obliged to contribute towards the support of the country only one-quarter of what his capital earned him above seven per cent is a pretty good kind of investor to keep clear of. I think that we do not want that kind of investor in Canada-he has too big an appetite for this Canadian land of ours.
Then the hon. gentleman showed a great deal of concern for the Canadian Pacific Railway. Several of the hon. gentlemen opposite have shown a marked solicitude, a new-found solicitude, for the Canadian Pacific Railway, and once again it strikes me that they are more solicitous for the interests of the Canadian Pacific Railway than the Canadian Pacific Railway is for itself. I believe that, owing to causes produced by this war, owing to the fact that they have carried a great many troops and an immense amount of supplies for the Government, that their telegraph systems have earned a great deal more because of these war conditions, and that their railway lines have made enormous profits out of freight rates, the directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway will be the first to admit the justice of their contributing a portion of these extra profits towards the maintenance of this country. No institution in Canada. I believe, has done more to develop the Dominion of Canada than has the Canadian Pacific Railway; and no company in Canada has received more benefit from its development than has this same company. It was not many years ago that the country looked to the Canadian Pacific Railway to perform a great national task, looked with confidence to the Canadian Pacific Railway to perform a task of inestimable importance to this country, and in spite of the sneers and the scorn of the Liberal party of this country, from the Pacific to the Atlantic, the Canadian Pacific Railway went forth and discharged that duty. At the present time the country looks to the Canadian Pacific Railway to do its duty again in a cause only more serious, and I believe they will not look in vain. It is abundantly clear from this debate that the Liberal party in Can-691
ada has decided to throw down the food producers in this country, the farmers and the fishermen. There was a time when hon. gentlemen opposite were on very good terms, or pretended to be, with the producers of foods in this country. They were the great friends of the farmer and, true to their policy of stirring up one class against another, they attempted to stir the farmer of Canada up against the inhabitant of the city, the employee in the industries; and they tried to make the farmer believe that he was being bled white by the manufacturers, by the city men. Fortunately, to-the credit of the farmer be it said, they were unsuccessful in that effort. The farmers and the fishermen of Canada recognized the fact that there must be various classes of people in this country if this country was to strive, that there must be factories as well as farms; and they refused to yield to the appeals of hon. gentlemen opposite, and hon. gentlemen opposite, -in despair, have decided now to change their tactics. The hon. member for Halifax frankly admitted a year or two ago that he had taken a census of the two and found in Canada more consumers than producers of food; and so his party has decided to throw down the producer of food, the fishermen and farmer, and to make a strong bid for the votes of the consumer. So he has discovered that food, farm products and fish, are too expensive in Canada, and too expensive by reason of the taxes and duties, and he says that if these duties were removed these foods would be cheaper. That is the policy that hon. gentlemen opposite now present to the country. In this particular debate it is the matter of potatoes that claims the attention particularly of the hon. member for Halifax. He expressed a great deal of scorn and indignation at the Minister of Finance for not exercising the power which he has of suspending the duty on potatoes and allowing American potatoes to come into this country free of duty, in order that the price of potatoes might be reduced to the consumer. Potatoes are expensive in this country at the present time, particularly in eastern Canada, for the reason assigned yesterday by the hon. member for Prince, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes).
Potatoes are expensive in Canada to-day because of the fact that last year there was an almost -total failure of the potato crop. There were only about one-quarter of the potatoes grown in Nova Scotia last year that arejisually grown there, and by reason

of that fact the price is juist twice as high as it was last year. The loss which followed from a shortage of the crop is made up half by the farmer and half by the consumer. Is that not perfectly fair? But my hon. friends opposite would put the entire burden on the farmers, and wouild compel them to sell the potatoes at the price which they would have got if the crop had been a full one. Is that fair to the farmer?
My hon. friends opposite object very seriously to the imposition of an increased tariff on apples. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) objected to the imposition of this duty on the ground that it will not benefit the fruit growers in the province of Nova Scotia. Even if that assertion were correct, I would conceive that it might still he in the interests of the people of Canada to impose such a tariff, because I believe that, in these matters, there should be no sectional or provincial feeling, but that they should be judged from the standpoint of the greatest good to the whole community. But my hon. friend is absolutely wrong when he says that the imposition of an increased tariff bn apples will not benefit the condition of the fruit growers in Nova Scotia, I am prepared to admit that the fruit grower in Nova Scotia stands in a somewhat better position than the fruit grower of Ontario or of British Columbia.
I believe that apples can be grown more cheaply in Nova Scotia than in any other part of the country, and I believe that they can be grown better. Besides, the apples of Nova Scotia are grown nearer to a great market, the British market, and therefore it' is quite possible that the fruit grower in Nova Scotia does not need protection so much as the fruit grower in other parts of Canada. But the prices during the last few years have gone down, and there is no money in fruit growing at the present crisis, and that fact has convinced them that there is a necessity for some such step as has been taken by the Minister of Finance. I have had a number of letters from fruit growers in Nova Scotia all of whom are entirely in favour of the change and heartily grateful to the Minister of Finance for proposing it.
I think, Sir, that it is a tremendous tribute to the statesmanship of this Government that they have shown so much concern for the farmer. I do not believe that any government in the Dominion of Canada, ever showed as much concern for the farmer as the present Government have shown, and I think that that fact is very

much to its credit, and a very great tribute to its statesmanship at the present time. If this country is to recover from the strain of this war, if it is going to be a great and glorious country, as we believe it is, its greatness and its glory must, at first, be largely achieved by the development of agriculture. We have great agricultural possibilities, and as soon as we can induce our own people to flock to the farms in greater numbers, as soon as we can attract greater immigration from . abroad to the farms, our country will begin to prosper. The Government cannot be better employed than in developing rural mail deliveries and parcel post, and in building good roads and extending the other favours that the present Government have extended to the farmer. They cannot be better employed than in making the agricultural industry popular with the people, because there is a great deal of truth in the statement of the American orator that if you burn down the cities and leave the farms, the cities will spring again as if by magic; but if you destroy the farms, it will not be long before the grass will grow in the city streets.
Hon. gentlemen opposite object to an insufficient reduction of expenditure by the present Government. A Government should keep a level head in respect to such matters at the present time. Often it is the poorest economy to cut down expenditures; there is truth in the saying that too rigid an economy is often the greatest extravagance. The hon. member for Halifax stated that the credit of this country was being destroyed by the fact that the Government were not making more radical reductions in expenditures. I would like to have asked the hon. gentleman, if he had been present, if he really thinks that this country would improve its credit by allowing its public works to fall into disrepair, by allowing them to remain unfinished, or by breaking contracts. I would ask hon. gentlemen opposite if our credit would not be injured by that sort of procedure rather than by going forward in a sensible and courageous manner to finish those public works. My hon. friend from Halifax gave an instance to show that the increased expenditures were affecting our credit prejudicially. This is what he said:
When the Minister of Finance made his loan of $45,000,000 in New York last July, I understand that J. P. Morgan & Company sent their representatives here to investigate the revenues and expenditures of the country. Street rumour has it that they were astounded at the vast sums of money expended in this country for unproductive purposes.

That is what the financial critic of the Opposition, speaking for his party, said in this House. There is no hon. gentleman _ on the opposite side of the House who makes a greater pretense to be fair than the hon. member for Halifax. Had the hon gentleman believed the truthfulness of this rumour it would have been hardly dignified, or patriotic to have quoted to the detriment of his country's credit without careful investigation. But as a matter of fact, the hon. gentleman had under his hand at the time evidence to show that this street gossip, if it existed, was absolutely wrong. What are the facts? After Mr. Morgan, or his agents, had made the investigation which they are reported to have made, he loaned this country money on most favourable terms. The bonds of this country were bought by him at a price, I think, from 99i to 99i, and only a few weeks afterwards, when the Anglo-French loan was floated, the combined credit of France and Great Britain could only command from this same capitalist a price of 96R
That proves conclusively that there was absolutely nothing in the street rumour, and it is a splendid tribute to the credit of this country, and to the way in which this loan was managed, that these Canadian bonds sold at a much higher figure than bonds of two such great financial powers as Great Britain and France.
One of the methods of reducing the expenditure which my hon. friend suggested was to curtail the advertising. He said that too much money was being distributed among the papers supporting the Government. I wish to say that in my judgment advertising is a poor item to practise economy on. I think that every business house in the country will agree that this is the last thing to curtail in. I know of no Government that ever invested money more wisely in advertising than did the present Government last year. How did they spend that money? One item of expenditure was in regard to advertising the advantages of the apple, in order to encourage the use of apples. Will hon. gentlemen say that that expenditure should not have been incurred? Another expenditure was incurred in conducting the " patriotism and production " campaign. Will the hon. gentlemen object to that expenditure? In speaking of unnecessary expenditures, the hon. gentleman says:
For instance, witness the large amount disbursed last year for advertising and printing to the press which supports the ministry.
Why did he confine criticism to the distribution of money to the press which supports the Ministry? I would like to ask hon. gentlemen opposite if money paid to the Government press is any greater strain upon the treasury than money paid to the Opposition press. While hon. gentlemen opposite have no objection at all to money being distributed amongst the Opposition press, they have a great deal of fault to find with the distribution of money amongst the press which supports the Government.
How much was distributed to the Opposition press?

I am not able to tell the hon. gentleman how much, but it was a very considerable sum, and I can tell him also that the very gentleman who made the criticism, the hon. junior member for Halifax, was one of the beneficiaries of this kind of advertising and that both of the papers owned by him, which are very much opposed to the Government at the present time-whether they are doing the Government any harm or not is another question- have received considerable amounts on account of advertising.
The hon. gentleman also asserted that the Post Office Department should be run in a much more economical manner I want briefly to refer to the items which account for what may be regarded as increases in the post office expenditures. I find that the expenditures for the year ended March 31, 1915, were greater than the expenditures for the previous year by about $3,000,000. I find that this increased expenditure is practically accounted for by four items: conveyance of mails by land, conveyance of mails by railway, salaries by cheques, and rural mail boxes. These four expenditures account for an increase of $3,068,214.73. Let us examine these items. First, there is the conveyance of mails by land. What was the cause of that expenditure? The cause of that expenditure was the introduction of rural mail delivery. Will hon. gentlemen object to that? As a matter of fact, when the proposal was before the House hon. gentlemen opposite did not give it their opposition. The second item is the conveyance of mails by railway. That is due to the introduction of the parcel post. For a number of years the railway companies had been claiming that the basis upon which they were paid was unsatisfactory. That matter went along for quite a while, but with the introduction of parcel post this Government had to

make new terms with the railway companies, with the result that this expenditure was incurred. But hon. gentlemen opposite did not object to the introduction of the parcel post system. Another item is in connection with salaries paid by cheques to outside officials of the department. This increase was due to two or three Acts which passed this House since the change of Government, providing for increased salaries for outside employees, and no member on the other side of the House voted, against one of these Bills. The fourth item is for rural mail boxes, which the Government have purchased to the amount of $450,000, and which sum they will get back again from the users of the boxes. Hon. gentlemen opposite talk about being fair. Personally I try to be fair, and I admire fairness in debate, but the brand of fairness that prompts hon. gentlemen to support legislation in this House calling for expenditure, and which then leads them to criticise the Government for making the expenditure under such legislation, is a brand of fairness that will not appeal to this House or to the country.
I am amazed at hon. gentlemen criticising particularly that item of expenditure in the Post Office Department under the head of " Conveyance of mails by land." They contend that these contracts now are let at enormous rates, without competition, and that they are let to others than the lowest tenderers. I can speak but for my own constituency, but in that constituency there is not a case where a contract for carrying the mails has been given to other than the man who agreed to do it for the least money, and I do not believe there is any hon. gentleman opposite who can cite a solitary case to the contrary anywhere in Canada. I believe that in every instance the contracts have been awarded by the Post Office Department to the people who have agreed to carry the mails for the lowest amount. After all, do hon. gentlemen want to make this country believe that the mail couriers are getting too much for their services? If there is one class of people in Canada who are underpaid, it seems to me that they are the people who carry the mails. Hon. gentlemen opposite have a great deal of sympathy for companies with a capitalization of over $50,000 who do not get more than seven per cent on their investment, but I would like them to point out to me in all Canada a single mail courier who gets seven per cent upon his investment. Hon. gentlemen have oceans of tears for interests with a $50,000
fMr. Davidson.]
capitalization who do not get seven per cent upon their investment, but they have not even a sigh fbr the poor courier who, in .rain and shine, in winter and summer, bumps over the rocks in some oases for fifty cents a day. This is not the first time we have heard hon. gentlemen opposite complain of the Government's extravagance, and demand a reduction in expenditure. Only a few months before this war broke out, when the Minister if Militia, with prophetic vision, was trying to prepare Canada for the calamity of war in which we are engulfed to-day, hon. gentlemen opposite from the member from Halifax down, criticised the Government for its militia expenditures. They occupied the time of this House for hour after hour, criticising the Government for introducing the military system into Canada, and protesting against the expenditure on the militia. I do not wish to say that hon. gentleman were disloyal in that course. I do not believe they said what they said with a full knowledge of the seriousness of it; but I think they are bound to admit now that they were wrong; that the words they used on them if they had any effect at all, had the effect of throwing obstacles in the way of the Minister of Militia, who was patriotically going about his duty of preparing the country for the peril. And I think hon. gentlemen opposite ought to reason with themselves that if their utterances on that occasion were so exceedingly unfortunate, there is also a very strong possibility that their words to-day may be equally mischievous.
The other night we listened with a great deal of pleasure to the eloquent remarks made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and it strikes me that what made those words of his grip our very hearts was the fact that they were in agreement with every public act of his, with every public utterance he has made during his long and useful public career. I think hon. gentlemen who heard those words of eloquence and high resolve must have been reminded of other words which the Minister of Trade and Commerce had used only a few months before in closing an important speech in an important debate:
In the event of such a contingency, and if the day of Armageddon came and caught us napping, I would like to have the consciousness that I am free from the remorse which would lie heavily upon me if I had been party to or contributed in that fatal delay.
Mr. Speaker, Armageddon is here, and there is no responsibility on the Minister

of Trade and Commerce, there is no responsibility on this Government, there is no responsibility on members on this side of the House. But what about the other side of the House?

What about
Drummond and Arthabaska?
Does not the hon. member for Red Deer realize that a tremendous responsibility rests upon him?
I think a great deal more responsibility rests upon the Minister of Trade and Commerce for his action in. the Drummond and Arthabaska by-election.

If in the light of what has taken place, if the hon. member for Red Deer and other hon. gentlemen opposite do not possess remorse, I say the Opposition are a lazaretto of incurables whose sensibilities have been deadened by a leprosy, and I am afraid their case is hopeless.
Why did you dismantle the Niobe?

Because, like the opposition that is put up by hon. gentlemen opposite, it was absolutely no good and of no benefit whatever. I am sorry if I have said anything to cause heart burnings among hon. gentlemen opposite. If they would only admit their folly, I would forgive them with a glad heart. Notwithstanding the mistakes hon. gentlemen opposite have made in the past, and which in their heart of hearts I believe they sincerely grieve over now, the country, thank God, is to-day united from the Atlantic to the Pacific, united in consciousness of our right, united in loyalty to the Empire, united in the determination to endure whatever hardships may come before us until the day of victory dawns.
Mr. LUCIEN T. PACAUD (Megantic): Mr. Speaker, I have listened with curiosity, if not with surprise, to the speech of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Davidson) who has just taken his seat. I had previously listened to a speech delivered this afternoon by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Boulay), and it is this latter speech which I should like to answer in a few words. It strikes me that, were we to analyse the speech of the hon. member for Rimouski, there would - be perhaps only three observations to make. In the first place, the hon. member was against the participation of Canada in the wars of the Empire before the war started:
to-day, when the war is on, he tolerates its existence, at which I am sure every hon. member will be very much gratified; and thirdly, the observation which seems to crown the other two is that he intends to continue to support the Government as he has done in the past, without any wavering and without any scruples of conscience. As this is the first occasion I have had of speaking in this House on the great issue which overshadows all others to-day, perhaps I may be permitted to lay special, stress on a few considerations which have impressed me still more deeply since the beginning of this debate. In the month of August, 1914, at the very outset of the greatest conflict known in history, the Canadian people, listening alike to the voice of reason and of sentiment, did not hesitate in the course which they intended to follow. Every province of this Dominion came forward spontaneously and patriotically and offered their best in men and in money. They understood, Sir, that if civilization, if justice, if liberty as we have conceived it, were to be maintained as the guiding star of our future destinies, a new and powerful enemy which had challeneged these lofty conceptions of human standard and opposed to them a new creed as hollow as it was barbarous, and which may be summarized in three words " Might is right," had to be crushed and crushed forever. In a word, we knew and felt, as we know and feel to-day, that in entering into this great struggle Canada was fighting not only for Canada, she was fighting not only for the Empire, but, above all, to maintain in this world all the great moral forces menaced, imperilled, and opposed by the German conception of "brute force." But, while from the very first our vision has been clear as to the justice of our cause, and as to the part we must take to insure its ultimate triumph, the speech delivered by the hon. Minister of Finance in this House a few days ago has revealed to us a situation which, if not sufficient in its gravity to deter us from our course-our national character knows not such weakness as to be deterred from the true course -has nevertheless stirred the public mind of this country to demand a radical and immediate change in so far as our national expenditure is concerned.
Let us stop for a moment to consider a single feature of the financial statement. We shall have added to our public debt in the short space of three years the enormous sum of $485,000,000. To understand the true meaning of these figures we can do
