no better than to compare them with the public debt of Canada in 1914, just previous to the war. The public debt at that time, which represented all our capital expenditures, which represented the cost of most of our great national enterprises, which covered a period of over fifty years of our national life, reached only $335,000,000. In the space of three years, at the end of the fiscal year 1917, the public debt will, in all probability, have reached $1,000,000,000, with the corollary that we shall be obliged to raise annually nearly $50,000,000 to meet the interest on that debt. In the face of such enormous expenditures is there not good reason for the serious reflection of every member of this House? Are we not justified in pleading with the Government for economy and for still more economy in so far as our civil Estimates are concerned? This appeal was made to the Government last year; it is repeated this year with equal force and with equal justification. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) a few days ago admitted, in his admirable and eloquent speech, that there were expenditures now, that there had been expenditures from Confederation up, which had been put in the Estimates, which had been passed by this House, which had been carried by this country, but which were neither useful nor expedient. If such expenditures, if such waste of the people's money were tolerated in the past, we were surely at fault; but, to-day, in this our hour of trial, when the people of Canada are more heavily taxed than they have ever been taxed before, when the sword of Damocles seems to hang over the head of every business man in this country in the form of new taxation, unjust, unfair and arbitrary, as during this debate it has been proved to be, it would be no less than a crime to continue in the old system which appears to us to-day in its true and hideous colours. Yet the Government continues in its extravagant course. For the coming year the Estimates for our ordinary expenditures will reach the sum of $159,000,000, the largest figures since Confederation. The hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) demonstrated clearly that millions of dollars could be saved. He singled out in the Estimates items which should be set aside; he mentioned others which should be considerably reduced; but there is an old saying which seems to apply to the present Government:
' There are none so deaf as those who will 
not hear." The Government should, in the face of a national crisis, have the courage to rise to a height where the evil influence of party patronage will lose its sway and relax its grip; or, will the Government continue as they have been doing in the past, alternating between a menace and a submission, one day full of fight, threatening the [DOT] Canadian people with a general election, very much against their will, the next day miraculously transformed, having become so meek and mild that they cannot muster sufficient courage to shoulder in whole or in part their responsibility in the creation of our shell committees. May I suggest that this continual vacillation on the part of the Government is not at all in keeping with the strenuous times which we are now confronting.
I now come to another point. I have heard it said and repeated many times that the province of Quebec has not done her share in this war; that she has not lent a sympathetic ear to the appeals of the recruiting agent. This asertion is false; it has no foundation in fact; it was launched and spread throughout this country by a few, fortunately only a few, whose narrowness of mind is a continual danger to our country. In a previous debate we heard what the province of Quebec had accomplished in this war, and it is needless for me to repeat it. It is sufficient for me to tell this House that my province has remained true to herself; that her devotion and loyalty to the British Crown has not wavered; that she is in this war with all her heart and soul. Let us not minimize the part that the province of Quebec has taken in this war. Let us in this country, on the contrary, welcome with pride the part that the old province of Quebec has played. If the facts were known, I think that every hon. member would accept the statement that I have just made.
For six years the province of Quebec witnessed the bitterest of political agitations. The French Canadians were told, day in and day out, that Canada should not. take part in any wars of the Empire, but that the obligations of our country were limited by our own boundaries. This was the language used; these were the sentiments uttered; these were the doctrines of the Nationalist party. This campaign of hatred and prejudice may have succeeded in winning a few more votes, it may have resulted in the downfall of a political party, it may have helped this Government to attain office; but let us take off our hats and be

proud that the French Canadians had a loyalty which these gentlemen could not shake.
Who were the leaders and who the followers of that party? Let us go down the long and well-known list. It is hardly conceivable, and yet it is true, that in this list we find two cabinet ministers, representing the province of Quebec in this Government, sharing in the responsibilities of conducting this war, and pursuing a policy which for six years they had openly and violently criticised and condemned- In this list we find at least twenty members sitting in this House, supporting this Government whom they were sent here specially for the purpose of defeating. I touch upon these points, not for the purpose of raising old issues-this is not the time for that-but to show what difficulties had to be surmounted in my province, what prejudices had to be overcome; and to show also what doubts have arisen in the minds of those who live in my province, when they see that the men coming before them are speaking in favour of taking part in this war are now the happy possessors of cabinet portfolios, who when they were ordinary representatives of the people condemned absolutely the very views that they aTe propounding to-day in the province of Quebec. The hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Blondin) has not yet told us in this House by what means he achieved the remarkable feat that has marked him out in our province as a political acrobat of no mean talent. The Minister of Inland Revenue (Mt. Patenaude) on the other hand, has tried to explain.. He spoke, but his words did not convey to us that which we had the right to expect, a full and sincere confession. He preferred to draw a veil over the many political heresies which he had propounded in the province of Quebec; and he concluded his remarks with a plea to the House and to the country for us all to forget and forgive. No, the province of Quebec will not forget, nor will it forgive. The day of chastisement has not yet come. I know the old province of Quebec well enough to know that it will remain true to its past traditions. It will not be turned from its course by any just anger it may have against these ministers who misrepresent it in this Government or against the members behind the Government. The people of Quebec will continue to fight for Canada and the Empire. But the day will come when the cannon's- Toar will cease, when the threat of German
world-dominion will be a thing of the past; the day when Canadians will enjoy peace, liberty and freedom at home, and the people will get together to work for the upbuilding of our common country; when the English and the French languages will be put on the same footing and will be taught freely without difference. And when that day comes, the day when we shall enjoy in this country the blessings of that happy culmination of liberty regulated by law, and law enlightened by liberty,-then, I say, will come the day when just punishment will be meted out to those who so richly deserve it.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I followed with great attention the speech of the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Boulay) this afternoon, and I must say that I was at a loss to understand his views on the important subjects dealt with in the Budget. The hon. member for Rimouski seems to represent the views of his electors every time he speaks against the Government. When he speaks he finds fault either with the individual ministers or with the general policy of the Government, but when the time to vote comes he gets up and votes for the Government. It appears, to me that when he is speaking in the House he represents the views of his electors, but when he is voting he represents the views of the hon. member for Rimouski. My hon. friend has taken the trouble to state that he visited St. John during the past summer and inspected the port there. He has visited and has seen many things, and there are many things he has not seen; there are many things he has seen and not understood, and no doubt while he saw the port of St. John, he did not understand whether it was a good seaport or not. The Minister of Marine and Fishery may not have understood all that my hon. friend said about the port of St. John, but I feel sure that the hon. minister will be able to look after that port when the time comes. There is one thing that we may always expect from the hon. member (Mr. Boulay), and it is that he will be glad to and ready to vote a big estimate for the development of the port of St. John every time he has an opportunity. I followed closely, also, the speech of the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson). I was amused at his remarks in reference to the hon. member from Maisonneuve (Mr. COMMONS
Verville). My friend from Maisonneuve represents the labour class in this House, and this afternoon he delivered a thoughtful and earnest address upon the subject of the extremely high cost of bread and the hardship it entailed on the working man; but yet my hon. friend from Annapolis said that the hon. member had not obeyed his mandate as a labour man in this House. I can assure the hon. member from Annapolis that the hon. member for Maisonneuve will return to this House next Parliament, and that there is a great probability that there will be more labour members, from the province of Nova Scotia, in that Parliament.
I was much interested in the remarks of the Minister of Finance during his Budget speech, but I shall discuss only a few of the important subjects which most deeply concern the country at this hour. We have lately been spending large sums; we have been sending our soldiers to the front and taxing ourselves for that purpose, and our generosity has no limit. We are again called upon to tax the Canadian people heavily in order to meet the heavy expense of keeping our soldiers at the front. Canada is better known to-day than before this war, simply because in Flanders and in France no nation striving for liberty and freedom has done more than our Canadian soldiers. Soon there will be an end to this great struggle, I hope, and what have we done to prepare for the return 'of our soldiers? Many speeches have been delivered in the country during the last summer by the ministers, and not one of them, omitted to point out the great importance of having a large immigration come to Canada after the war. Before we look for immigration into this country after the war, we should put the country in a good financial position, we should look after our natural resources and prepare to take care' of the widows and orphans of our soldiers on the conclusion of the war. I have been interested since the war began in what I may term national economy. Go into any city in Canada to-day and you find no difference in the way of living amongst the rich class of people, the class of people who have a fair revenue from year to year. It is the poorer class of people who are making the greatest sacrifices during this conflict. It is the poorer people who are really bearing the great burden of the war. We have increased the cost of their living by increasing the tariff, but we have never for a moment thought of increasing their salaries or wages in order that they may bear the increased burden of the cost of 
living. The sons of the labour man and of the farmer are in the majority in the trenches to-day. A great number of them will soon come back, I hope, and what arrangements have we made for them on their return? The attention which is to-day being devoted to immigration should be given entirely to these returning soldiers, their wives and their children. It is the children of our soldiers who will, in the near future, partly decide the destiny of this country. Among the soldiers who have enlisted from my own town there are two who have left families, one of eight children and another of seven. All they have fox their support for the moment is the pay of their fathers and what is given them from the Patriotic Fund. For the present that is very satisfactory; but let us look into the future. What happens to these children if their fathers fall on the field of battle? They will have mothers who are poor, left to look after them, and I say it is a deplorable position for these families if the country does not at once fake steps to look after them. Let us not depend too much on immigration from Europe after the war. The soldiers of Britain, France, Belgium, Serbia, and other countries who have joined the Allies, will not be permitted to oome to Canada after the war. Those who are between the ages of 18 and 45 will be needed at home, they will have to return to the soil and to industrial pursuits. They will have to rebuild the country devastated by the enemy, and I predict' that for a long while we in this country will have a very small immigration. We do not want any one above the age of 40 or 50 coming into the country, not do we want any one below 18. We do not want orphans and widows, and I repeat, that we will be greatly disappointed in out expectations of immigration after the war from the countries now engaged in this struggle. What will be our financial standing after the war? A year from now we will have a debt of one billion dollars.
What is true of the different nations of Europe is also true of Canada in reference to what will happen after the war. I have in my possession the opinion of an American subject. It is given in an article entitled " A Glimpse at the Future," and is as follows:
The demand for capital will not increase (in, the aggregate) in Europe after the war, but' will decline. It will decline absolutely, far more than the supply. For this reason interest rates will more likely fall to a low level and remain there for a long time, rather than rise or even hold at the relatively high levels ex-

isting during the actual hostilities while the government are floating their big loans. A -[DOT] demand for capital " means a producer whose market has so broadened that he can profitably borrow money to increase his producing capacity; or it means that his customers are buying so freely that he needs to carry a larger stock of goods. In short, it means, for business generally, an enlarged demand for goods. Now the direct effect of war is not to increase demand or buying capacity, but rather to impoverish a country to such an extent that people everywhere buy less of everything. In consequence, producer, dealer and transporter all have less to do, and because of this none of them need much or any new capital. Consequently, demand for capital falls flat and interest rates range at low levels.
If this is the case, it is another reason why we should go slowly when we consider what will happen after the war is over and what is now best to be done. Sir George Paish said lately:
The money which has not been saved constitutes an enormous loss. That may be said to be gone for ever. The loss of the greater part of the world's entire savings for even eighteen months is a very serious matter and its seriousness will become more and more intense the longer the war lasts and the period of loss extends.
I say then, Mr. Speaker, that when war was declared, this Government should have given an example of economy. Parties found guilty of handling improperly public money should have been punished. The man found with goods belonging to the Canadian people should be punished. Companies organized for the purpose of manufacturing munitions of war at a profit greater than that of an ordinary business firm should not be tolerated. The high cost of living should be studied, and a remedy at once applied in order to help out those who have not a sufficient revenue to support their families in comfort.
If this war should unfortunately make many Canadian millionaires, it will be a sad page in the history of Canada. The future generation, the sons of our soldiers who are at the front, will be called upon to pay the war debt, and it would be a pity to see them living alongside the sons of millionaires who had made their fortunes out of war munitions.
I read with surprise a report of the failures in the United States during the year 1915. There were 19,035 reported, an increase of 13.4 per cent over 1914. Our big neighbours to the South of us are certainly showing us an example in the matter of preparing for the future and of practising economy. In a country like the United States, which has received from the Allies millions of dollars on war contracts,-and
which had only an average crop last year, it is not surprising that the question of the high cost of living has arisen, and it will have to be solved there in the same manner as in Canada.
The Government have endeavoured to do their duty in every manner possible in reference to helping out the Mother Country and the Allies in this great war. The fathers, mothers, young men, and young women of this country are doing all they can. The Canadian people have shown a noble example to the world, and have done their duty with cheerfulness, and in the true spirit of patriotism. We should, Sir, at this very moment study what is one of the greatest questions in Canada to-day, the question of national economy. We should endeavour to find a remedy to meet the conditions that will arise after the war. We will certainly do ourselves a great injustice if we do not prepare just now for the future. We are not anxious to disturb the public mind, but the public mind has been disturbed, already by the high cost of living, and if a remedy is not applied immediately we will have, in the future, great hardships amongst the poorer classes of Canada. When the times were prosperous a man earning $1.75 or $2 a day could very well afford to pay for the necessaries of life, but now he is earning $1.50 and $1.75 a day and has to face an increase of between forty and fifty per cent in the cost of living. So that, if things go on in the same way, we will be called upon before long to take down the wall of protection an^ to give free entry to foodstuffs into Canada in ordeT to meet the requirements of the poorer classes.
At the beginning of the war the Canadian people were rather taken by surprise when our boys were called upon to take -up arms and to cross the ocean, but since then there has grown1 a feeling of determination, and the people have just one object in view, and that is to see our great armies triumph over our enemies.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know that I can add anything to what has been said by hon. members on both sides of the House in regard to what is known as the Budget. It is a practice and a right guaranteed to members of a legislative body like ours that in the Budget debate we can roam far afield in the discussion and deal with any question that we think appertains to the welfare of the people of the country.

It is right that that should be so, because on the matter of the speech of the Finance Minister depends the financial future of the country. He is supposed to be the balance wheel, financially, at least, in the Government, and he is. expected to keep in subjection the unruly members of that body. Those who desire to spend money which they have not, and which they see no way of getting except by pressing the Finance Minister to make another loan, are supposed fo listen to the warnings of the Finance Minister, if he gives those warnings, and to keep the expenditure within the limits which he, in his judgment, says the finances of the country are able to stand. I regret that, with the present Government, either the Finance Minister is not sufficiently strong, or the members are too unruly, because he has not been able to keep them in subjection as far as their expenditure is concerned. Even this session they ask to have a statute passed to expend $28,000,000 more than the Finance Minister tells us ought to be spent. We have tried, as each minister presented his Estimates, to induce him to meet the demands of the Finance Minister by telling the House frankly whether he, in his department, intends to synchronize his expenditure with the statement of the Finance Minister. Up to date no member of the Government has agreed, in so far as his expenditure is concerned, with the statement of the Finance Minister. Even the docile Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) refuses to have his Estimates cut down to the extent of $500. When such a quiet-mannered member of the Government as the head of the Justice Department will not agree to have his expenditure reduced even a little to meet the requirements of the Minister of Finance, what, oh what, can be expected of the large spending departments?
The Minister of Finance, in his remarks, dealt briefly and succinctly with questions of vital interest to the country at the present moment, and with the problems that have confronted us, do confront us and will increasingly confront us for some years to come. He spoke of the loan by which Canada borrowed $45,000,000 in the United States. There possibly were two reasons for going to the United States. One reason was to regulate, as far as possible, the difficult question of exchange, and the other was, if I may hint it mildly, that the atmosphere in the Old Land had grown quite cool when it came to borrowing for domestic purposes even by Canada. I 
believe it is not going too far afield to say that at the time this money was required, it was the opinion of the money market in England that Canada should adopt other means in order to finance her own domestic affairs because the burden on the Motherland in financing herself, in granting the aid which she has given to Canada, and in assisting some of the Allies, was already sufficiently great for even that great centre of financial strength to assume. I am not sure that the Finance Minister made a very good bargain in connection with that loan. I read carefully the terms of the provincial loan by the Hon. Thomas McGaa-ry, and, comparing them, I rather think, to put it in ordinary language, that he got a shade on the Finance Minister in a transaction that he made with the New York financiers. The loan made by the Dominion of Canada in New York was ostensibly a short date loan coming due in 1917, but, as a matter of fact, these securities are negotiable for securities having a thirty-five year term at 5 per cent; so that if the New York investor desires, he can convert his short term loan into a long term one at the ordinary rate of interest of 5 per cent, which means that Canada expects to pay not less than 5 per cent for her money for the next thirty-five years. That is not as good an arrangement for Canada, in so far as the interest is concerned at least, as if it were a short term loan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Will my hon.
friend allow me to correct him? The bonds mature in 1935, but they are twenty-year bonds.

My statement with reference to the term then should be corrected by saying that the bonds are for twenty years. They mature in 1935, but you extend the term of this short loan for twenty years. Then there was the loan of $50,000,000 from the people of Canada. The Finance Minister asked for $50,000,000 but he got $100,000,000. The request that the people should hand into the treasury $50,000,000 met with such a hearty response that they doubled the amount. That shows that the people not only had the money, but they were willing to lend it to the Dominion Government, some of them to withdraw it from the other investments that were paying a higher rate of interest than the Government were proposing to pay which, I believe, is approximately 5J per cent considering the price of the security. I do not wish to criticise the Government on this point especially but I think it was hardly proper that, having

asked the people for $50,000,000, they should impound $50,000,000 more and make it $100,000,000. I know the Finance Minister will say to me: We sent a notice to every investor that we would al.'<:w him to v/ith-draw the amount of his subscription to this loan if he so desired, and thus it might have been reduced to $50,000,000, but that few, if any, did withdraw their subscriptions. One can see at a glance the position in which you place the investor. After having said to the Government: I will subscribe a certain amount, he could not very well, without placing himself in a peculiar position, withdraw that proposition and ask that his subscription should be smaller. I know that no public objection has been taken, and I am not taking serious objection to it, but financial men in discussing it will want to know the next time the Finance Minister asks for a certain amount if he is going to double up on it. They make their arrangements along certain lines and it must be remembered that some of these institutions withdrew investments that were paying a higher rate of interest in order to give the money to the Government at a lower rate of interest.
My hon. friend referred to the balance of trade but I hardly think that he will follow that argument to its logical conclusion. If the argument of my hon. friend be correct, then the longer this war lasts the better off Canada will be. The balance of trade to-day is diie to -the abnormal condition in which we find ourselves. It is not due to the natural development of trade; no person pretends it is. The Minister of Finance himself, I thought, made the wonderful admission-I think it has been practically repeated by every member who has spoken on that side of the House-that Canada, at the outbreak of the war, was in a critical position financially and industrially.
If I wished to say a word politically, I might say that it was a strong admission the Finance Minister made, that, after three years of the management of his Government Canada found herself in a more critical position than she had been since his party was in power before. As a matter of fact, everybody knows we were in a critical condition, both industrially and financially. Then the war broke out, and very large orders came for different kinds of war material. The balance of trade which the Finance Minister pointed to is due to these two things: first, the large crop in the West, and secondly the immense value of The war orders we have received. But my
hon. friend may say to me:	If you have
got the money for the grain and. the money for the war munitions, if your theory be correct, why don't you purchase imports and reduce the balance of trade? Sir, the world knows that the money received by Canada during the past year was not used to buy imports for the reason that, in the first place, they had to pay their debts of three years' standing, and secondly, the balance of the money received had to be devoted to the prosecution of the war; it is on account of these two things that the so-called balance of trade is in our favour. After all, this question of balance of trade might be argued for months and years, and it has ben so argued. Under normal conditions, if we import goods to take the place of a certain amount of goods we have exported to a foreign country, we are prosperous rather than otherwise. As outlined by the Finance Minister, we have this year a balance of trade of $200,000,000 in our favour, while some years ago we had an adverse balance. Now, I should like to ask any business man here which period in the history of Canada he would prefer: the present period with the so-called balance of trade in our favour, or the period of much greater prosperity a few years ago, when the so-called balance of trade was adverse. Theorists may theorize, but the fact is that when trade flows freely to and fro between countries, business is in a healthy condition. I do not think much of this balance of trade theory, because we, as a practical people, have to face in our every-day living conditions and not theories, and the history of our country shows that year after year prosperity has come to the high and the low, to the rich and poor, even when the so-called balance of trade was adverse.
The. Finance Minister gave us some good advice in his Budget speech, and I know he will pardon me if I read a paragraph to the House. On page 847 of Hansard, speaking of economy and economic conditions generally, he says:
From this viewpoint it is our true policy to augment our financial strength by multiplying our productive exertions, and by exercising a rigid economy which reduces to the minimum all expenditures upon luxuries and non-essentials. Only in this way shall we be able to make good the loss caused by the withdrawal of so many of our workers from industrial activities, repair the wastage of the war, and find the funds for its continuance. It cannot be too frequently or too earnestly impressed upon our people that the heaviest burdens of the conflict still lie before us, and that industry and thrift are, for those who remain at home, supreme patriotic duties upon which faithful fu'fliment

our sueess and consequently our national safety may ultimately depend.
Apart altogether from these higher grounds, it is to be pointed out that in so far as our present prosperity is based upon abnormal prices for our produce and upon the production of war material, it is precarious and transient, and dependent upon the continuance of the war and its conditions. On ordinary business grounds alone, the prudent husbanding of resources,- and the wise conservation of profits, are dictated by the plainest considerations of practical wisdom and good sense. It is in the spirit of these remarks that I now approach the consideration of our financial estimates and programme for the coming year.
I agree with every word of that. But the Government do not take to heart the good advice which they and the Finance Minister give to the rest of the people of Canada. They say to us: If you indulge in luxuries cut them out and buy only necessities, be economical; if you have made profits store them away. Now, I will put it to the Finance Minister-but no, I need not put it to him, for be has already admitted the soundness of my argument when he said that present conditions were precarious, and only temporary, and that we should provide for the future. But I will put it to the Minister of Marine, the Minister of Labour, or the Solicitor General: If the ordinary man in Canada ought to take the advice of the Finance Minister and cut out his luxuries would it not be wise for the heads of Government departments to do the same thing, and cut off luxuries from their Estimates? The Minister of Finance has undoubtedly pleaded with them in Council to do so, but they will not take his advice. The Finance Minister tells Parliament and the country that at least $30,000,000 of these Estimates are luxuries. I therefore ask the Government to follow the wise advice of their own Finance Minister, and before they pro' ceed any further with the Estimates to get together for the national good, and cut out the luxuries in these Estimates. As the Finance Minister well points out, it is only by sacrifices that we can hope to bear the burdens of the war, the heaviest of which are still ahead, and in that way only can we hope to retain our position in the world as a country that knows no stopping in its national progress. The Finance Minister, in his Budget speech, estimated the year's expenditure at $160,000,000. We see, however, that the civil expenditure is estimated at $158,000,000, and the capital expenditure at $30,000,000, or a total of $188,000,000. There is, therefore, a chasm between the Finance Minister's Estimate of

$160,000,000 and the $188,000,000 of $28,000,000. When speaking of the Estimates just now I said that, according to the Finance Minister $30,000,000 were luxuries; to be accurate I should have said $28,000,000. I have every confidence that the Minister of Finance intends to keep the expenditure down to $160,000,000; but, if it is true that he intends to do- so, why are we, as responsible representatives of the people, asked to place on the statute book a law which gives the ministers a right to expend $28,000,000 which the Minister of Finance says they ought not, in the public interest, to expend. This is a serious matter in any deliberative assembly, particularly at a time of such great stress, when every man, woman and child in this great land is straining every nerve to do his or her utmost, so that the boys we have sent to the front not only may win glory for themselves, but may help to retain for us the great privileges and birthrights for which our fathers fought. We are not living under ordinary circumstances when a great deal of elasticity might be permitted; we are living in 'a time when we are all doing our best, and if the Government of Canada expects the people to husband their resources and practice the economy which the Government preaches, it ought to show an example and take out of the Estimates the $28,000,000 which there is no need to expend during the coming year.
We have expended more money than we should have expended, and we have had a good deal of discussion about the methods of expenditure in conection with war supplies. I do not wish to dilate on these matters at any great length, because my desire is that we, as a Parliament, should not be divided in the schemes- which we are trying to work out for the nation's good. What I am saying, I am saying in the most serious way to- endeavour to impress upon the Government what I think to be its duty in this trying time. I need not argue that millions of dollars have been expended that might have been saved. The Government must realize that, and I think no person realizes it more than those who sit around the council board and talk these matters over, and have before them	details which we on the outside have not been privileged to -see, and only fragments of which have come* under our notice.	To show that the
method of buying war supplies has not been right, I need only call the Prime Minister and his colleagues as witnesses.

It will be remembered that at the outbreak of the war the Militia Department made the purchases of war supplies. The Prime Minister himself came to the conclusion that that method of purchasing was not satisfactory, and almost at the very outset he was so informed by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. Here is just one paragraph from a letter which Mr. Murray, secretary of the association, sent to the Prime Minister:
Stories that are going the rounds may have no foundation in fact, but the persistence with which they are being circulated, and the circumstantial detail with which they are being backed up, is creating a feeling of suspicion and distrust that is doing your Government real harm. I am quite prepared to believe that nothing, or at most very, very little, has been done to justify these suspicions, at the same time it would seem wise to remove all ground for suspicion by throwing the business wider open and by placing it in all instances with manufacturers direct instead of through middlemen.
The Minister of Militia in his recent speech in the House said that middlemen came to Ottawa by the score, and we all know that to be true. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association say that it was true, and, as they could not get at the buying department direct, if what Mr. Murray says is the truth, complaint was made to the Prime Minister. A little later on the Prime Minister must have agreed that there was something wrong with the method of purchasing, because he changed it and appointed a sub-committee of council, thus taking the work of purchasing out of the hands of the Militia Department in which it had previously been. That sub-committee took in hand the purchasing of war supplies and it was not long before some one found out that they were not equal to the task. To prove that, you need not take my word; you can take the word of the Government, practically of the Prime Minister himself, because he disbanded that sub-committee in a short time and appointed another, not confining himself to the members of the Government at all. I find that the Prime Minister had tried them all and found them all wanting, and that he said:	" If we want to do this
purchasing properly, we must go outside of the Government, because it does not seem to be made up of business men at all." Two-thirds or a majority of the board that was appointed is outside of the Government, and the chairman of the board is the hon. member for East Toronto (Hon. Mr. Kemp), Minister without Portfolio. I need not argue that the purchasing for many months was done improperly. The
action of the Prime Minister in dispensing with two organizations which he had formed for the purpose, and in appointing a third, proves my case more conclusively than if I talked for an hour. What has happened in Canada has started the Canadian people thinking, and the news which we received this evening shows that they are thinking. The issue in Peel county was solely on the point of the purchasing of supplies in the way of horse-flesh for our boys at the front, and to-day in that comparatively small county in Ontario a change of twelve hundred votes has resulted on th'at issue alone. What I am trying to convince the Government of at the present time is not of a political nature, but, the fact that the people of Canada have not been satisfied with the way in which the purchase of all kinds of war supplies has been conducted.

It is a hard pill to
swallow.

In regard to taxation; I admit at the outset that we must find some new method of taxation to meet the great responsibilities and to carry the great burdens that are at present resting upon us, and which, as the Minister of Finance says, will become greater in the future. We need not plume ourselves on the fact that we have what is called a favourable trade balance. In the years to come we shall have to face the most serious condition that Canada has ever faced, a much more serious condition than confronts us at present. .We cannot retreat; there is no Canadian worthy of the name who would think of retreating. There must be no retreat by Canada until we gain what we are attempting to gain in this great fight in which we, along with the Allies, are engaged. Our business is now not to act from a party standpoint in the hope of gaining political advantatge, but calmly to try to find how we can get the money which we need and how we can get it from the sources that ought to pay it, - and that we need the money goes without saying.
Taxation is never welcome, and seldom is it distributed with absolute equity. Under our municipal institutions the rate of taxation is the same for every tax-payer in the municipality, but even so the taxes may not be equitable as they depend upon the assessment valuation. In most instances, the man in ordinary circumstances pays a little more than his share of the municpal taxes. Mr. A. owns a house and lot that, all told

is worth $1,200 and if it were to be sold tomorrow it would probably bring $1,000. It is a practical house, with no extra finish and fit for the occupancy of a man in ordinary circumstances and the assessor will probably put down the value of that property at $1,000. But Mr. B has a house which cost $50,000, yet he will probably escape with an assessment of $20,000, on the ground -for which there is some reason-that there are so few possible purchasers for a property of that kind that if it were put on the market it would not bring more than $20,000. But that does not alter the fact that the system results in the ordinary ma^ paying more than his relative share of the municipal taxes. I do not believe that we can expect perfect equality in whatever taxation is imposed, but I do believe that the Finance Minister ought not to consider himself wedded to what he has proposed merely because the Government has proposed it. This is apart from and beyond any party measure and it is proposed under conditions that do not permit of partisan discussion of it. The Finance Minister ought to have an open mind on this subject, and if something better is proposed he ought to accept it and welcome it.
With that in mind, I am going to discuss some of what seem to me the glaring inequalities of this proposed taxation measure. I absolutely believe that the Finance Minister intends to change these things. I cannot conceive that he will adhere to his proposition as laid down after the full facts have come to him, as they must have come to him, if not in mail-bags full, at least in letter-boxes full, to say nothing of various deputations. And I want to impress it again on the Government before I leave the subject, that while they are asking the industries of Canada to contribute of their excess profit, they ought at once to cut off their own excess estimates. Let us get together, one paying and the other reducing expenditure, and then the burden will be evenly divided between the payer and the economist, if such there be in the Government. One objection is, that this is a proposal to tax industry while, to a great extent, it omits to tax. wealth. Wealth and water escape; industry and integrity get soaked.
With the water?

There is enough water in some of these concerns to soak out a lot of integrity. Let us consider the retroactive principle in this measure. I want it to be 
distinctly understood that I am not now dealing with any institution that has furnished war supplies and made an abnormal profit. I admit at once, and without a word, the contention that if the retroactive principle were not applied the Finance Minister would not get his money, because, if the Munitions Board is up to its business, then, in the year that is ahead of us, these concerns will not make any excess profit; and so, if the Finance Minister is to get from those who have made abnormal profits from war supplies a fair share of those profits, he must make the law 9 p.m. retroactive. In what I- have to say I have no reference whatever to those institutions that have made these abnormal profits as a result of the war. I say to the Government, tax them. It is their duty to contribute, and they ought to be willing to contribute a large share of these profits to further the great object we are striving for. But, in doing that, to use the words of an ancient writer, let no man escape. A good many will escape; but of that later. Let me point out to the minister the case of many industries which are not furnishing munitions or war supplies at all. I take one company as an illustration, without mentioning names. In 1912, 1913 and 1914 business with this concern kept getting a little worse all the time, and, before the war broke out, the company owed the bank quite a large amount of money. But the men who were in it were the kind of men that Canada wants. They were real business men. They did not flee for aid to some unknown source when they found they were coming to a time of stress. They did what the Government has not done, they reduced expenditures; they girded up their loins to face the situation. They had to reduce the time of their men to half-but giving all some employment that their families might be kept together. And they hoped against hope that the tide would turn. During the past year the company has made some money on account of the improvement in conditions. They have paid up the bank as well as they could, and to-day they are in a better position. But if the money they took to pay off their indebtedness to the bank is taxed as profit under this measure, these men will have to go and borrow that money, or at least a portion of it, from the bank again. That is not fair to the industry of the country. We ought to face this question, and so levy taxation that the money shall be paid by the men most able to pay it. Under the conditions which I

have described, the man who carried on the business for years, and who, it may be, has his son in the company with him, may have to go into bankruptcy unless this measure is changed. They have made more than their seven per cent, and they have paid the money back to the bank to which they owed it. They have not got a dollar of money on hand, and if they are compelled to go on their knees to the bank to borrow that money again, it will be unfair to industry, and will be a check to the commercial life of this country.
That is only one sample, and the minister will find that there are quite a number of similarly situated institutions in the Dominion. I cannot think that he has them in mind, and I urge upon him that, in a case of that kind, where a man who has been honestly working and struggling for years has gone to the bank and paid off his indebtedness, or part of it, dpring the last couple of years, thus enabling him to proceed with his business and keep his company together, that the Bill be so amended that some redress may be given to this man, and that he may escape a taxation which he is not able to bear, and should not be asked to bear. Take another class. Some are under the impression that money put into betterments or held in reserve will be allowed as capital. The proposed measure d,oes not say so, except as to small concerns, such as partnerships. In Ontario most businesses are put into the shape of joint stock companies for convenience, and because that ' is a better method of doing business. The men at the head of these companies are real business men; they are not mushrooms. Their business has not been carried on for kite flying in stocks, but has, perhaps, been carried on for years, handed down from father to son, carried on with honesty and integrity and with profit to the development of the whole country. What do these men find,? Year after year, it being their own business, they did not take the profits and put them in their pockets; they took what money they made, whether it was ten, or twelve, or fifteen per cent, and added betterments to their concerns. They bought new machinery, they were trying to fit themselves to compete with all comers. They built new buildings, brought in new apparatus, discarded old steam engines, and in some places put in electric power, adapted all modern methods of doing business successfully. What do we find under the proposed measure? These betterments,
these additions to their business, these improvements that have given employment to men in Canada, and will do so in the future, that have helped to make Canada what she is, a hive of industry; these things will be taxed under the Bill, and twenty-five per cent of the money put into these betterments, if the earnings are over seven per cent, will have to be handed back to the Government as taxes. The people of Canada who have money do not demand that from these people. Those in Canada who are able to pay for the carrying oh of this war are the last men who will demand that these businesses, worked up in the way I have mentioned, shall be taxed to that extent. I urge upon the Finance Minister that his measure be so changed that consideration will be given in the cases I have mentioned in respect to companies as well as to partnerships.
Companies that have head offices in Canada are being invited by this measure, as it now stands, to remove their head offices to another country. There are several businesses in Ontario, and undoubtedly quite a number in Canada, whose head offices are in this country, but the greater proportion of whose business is outside of this country. We are glad to have the head offices of these institutions in Canada. They are working under provincial or Federal charters, and the profits from all these sales, all over the world, come back to the Dominion of Canada and are largely spent here. But the interest, of these institutions, in many cases, lies nearly altogether in another country and the minister, by his present method of taxation, leaves it open to these companies to take out American charters and move their head offices across the line. In this way they will escape the taxation. I say that that is an invitation .to these companies to take away their head offices from Canada, and in some oases these are great institutions and it has been a great benefit to Canada to have their head offices here. I admit that it is easy to give advice to the Minister of Finance, but I am bringing these matters to his attention as strongly as I can because it cannot be worked out in an easy way; it will take time.
I come now to a class of people who escape this taxation altogether. As men get older they begin to retire from business, unless they are harnessed to it. Where do they put their money? They are tired of the risks of business, and so they buy bonds at six per cent or Government bonds at five and a half per cent. It



is not fair to compare the income from a six per cent bond or a five and a half per Cent Government bond with the income from a seven per cent return, from an industrial concern. The man who holds the bonds takes no risk, not a cent. The man who has his money in an industrial concern- at six or eight per cent is taking all the risk, and any day his whole capital may be wiped out. Perhaps a 'Government bond at five and a half per cent is equal, when we consider the element of security, to an income of about twelve per cent in an ordinary industrial concern. As men grow older they get away from the industrial concern; they want something safe and sound. Their chief occupation is to have an enjoyable life and to cut coupons to_keep life going on leisurely; so they buy Government bonds. In this country many vaults are full of municipal and Government bonds. A man may be worth $1,000,000 of Government or municipal bonds and not contribute one farthing under this Bill; while the man next to him may be of the same age but may be harnessed to his business, working hard with his sons in a small company, and he is taxed under this measure. I ask if that is equity. The fact that this is so proves what I said a moment ago that in that instance industry is taxed and wealth goes scot free. I would prefer absolutely an income tax, graded, and not imposed on small incomes where it would affect the living of any ordinary man, woman, or child. But these are abnormal times and we could perhaps hardly adhere to that principle, particularly in cases where large concerns have -made abnormal profits out of the war. '
Let me point out another inequality, and this, I know, will strike the Minister of Finance. We have one dry goods store here with a large capitalization, which is perhaps not taxed under this Bill; but the competitor of that concern, with a much smaller capitalization and not doing nearly the business, will have to pay twenty-five per cent of its excess profit over seven per cent. That is not fair; and there is no system of reasoning by which it can be argued that it is fair. A big concern which ordinarily buys cheaper and does a bigger trade and surely makes more money, will not, under this measure as it now stands, have to contribute a farthing under certain conditions; while its competitor, doing a smaller business, may have to contribute.
Then, take the manufacturing concerns.
fMr. Graham. 1
Under the Bill if passed, as proposed by the Minister of Finance, a boot and shoe concern, which I have in mind, will not contribute a farthing, while a competing boot and shoe company, a few blocks away, will pay, perhaps, $20,000. That is an inequality which the Government cannot afford to allow. I could go on citing instances, but I want to give a few concrete cases, and not at all with the view of criticising any company. I believe that every man in this country is willing to pay his share of taxation, but he wants to know that every other man, who is in a position to do so, will pay; and if the object of the Government is to have equality, they will have to change the Bill very radically.
Let me give a few instances. I think the figures I am about to cite are correct; they have been hurriedly got together, but I think they are approximately correct. Take the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and I am told that they object to the taxation on other grounds which I do not know to be the case, but the Canadian Pacific Railway, under this measure will pay over $2,000,000, while the Canadian Northern Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway, competing transcontinental lines, will pay nothing. If we are going to take into consideration what institutions or industries make out of war profits, I think you will find that every one of those railway companies has made a little out of this war. There are three transcontinental railway companies; one of them will pay over $2,000,000, and the other two, competing lines, will pay nothing. The Minister of ^Finance rather gloried in the fact that the farmers were not going to be taxed. Let me just say this: that every dollar you put on the railways will have to be paid by the individuals who use the railways.
. Mr. MEIGHEN: Out of the taxation of surplus profits?

The railways are going to have surplus profits next year just as they have had this year, and my hon. friend the Solicitor General cannot get away with that kind of quibble. When railways contribute anything, they find a way of getting back at the man who uses the railways, just as any payment made out of any concern will add a little to the price of the goods of that concern, and the consumer will ultimately pay.
Then we should never tax the railways at all.
You have not done it so far, but when you do tax them, you ought to tax them all; that is my argument.

That would be more
out of the pockets of the people.

Not at all; my hon.
friend is not very well versed in how the railways manage their affairs. For example, the Toronto Street Railway has a capital of $12,000,000, and it will pay approximately $88,000; the Quebec Railway, with a capital of $10,000,000, will pay nothing under the Bill as it was outlined by the Minister of Finance in his speech. What I am arguing is, that my hon. friend will have to change his Bill, even if he has to let go a good deal of his speech. The Solicitor General seems to be at variance with the Minister of Finance, for he says the Bill is going to be all right. What I am anxious to do is to impress upon the Government the inequalities of their proposed taxation as I see them. There is plenty of time to change the Bill and to make the taxation as equitable as possible.
The Ogilvie Flour Mills, with a capital of $4,500,000, will pay $201,000, while the Dominion Flour Mills, with a capital of $1,000,000, will pay nothing. There is another clause to which my hon. friend will have to give some attention, and, perhaps, make some variation in, and that is the mining clause. I am not here with a brief for the miners at all, but every man who knows anything about mining, as some of our hon. friends from the West and from Northern Ontario do, knows that a mine is a terminable quantity and that the returns from that terminable quantity are supposed to be sufficiently great that when the source of wealth is exhausted the mine will have returned to the owner his capital as well as a profit on his investment.
