There would be a grievous injustice, but if the minister intends to work that out in any way, and it will not be too easy to work it out properly, my criticism as far as the mining industry is concerned will be withheld until I see the Bill, which he has and I have not.
Having dealt with that, let me speak for a few moments concerning the great question that is before us; that is the question of why we are asking for all this money, of why we are worrying as to various methods of taxation in order to produce the best results. I fear that what I am going to say will not meet with the concurrence of a good many of my own friends and of many who have perhaps given the subject as much attention as I. In the press of Canada and in the speeches of some public men, the United States has been criticised for not being more aggressive under the circum? stances. Of course, it is none of our affair in a way what the United States may do as a country. As a neutral country they have a perfect right to take whatever action seems to them best, but speaking from the viewpoint of Canada, as I see it, the United States should not be condemned by any one in Canada for the attitude it has assumed. It is a terrible thing to plunge a great nation into war and there are so many conflicting interests, of which we in Canada possibly know nothing, or little, and so many contingencies that may arise did the United States declare war, or join with the Allies, that, I say, any man who carries the responsibility on his shoulders of the welfare of nearly 100,000,000 of people ought to hesitate long before he plunges that people into this great war. But, turning to the other side, as a Canadian, my view is that we would lose rather than gain if the United States should join the Allies as a combatant. What would happen? We are now getting large amounts of munitions and supplies from across the line. Suppose the United States entered actively into the war, the Supply of war materials for the Allies would, in a large measure, be stopped because the United States would have to

begin at once and equip an army of her own. She has no army of any great strength that could leave her shores. With a population of nearly 100,000,000 to-day her army is comparatively small - and it would take time to do what Canada has done-find, drill and equip an army before she would be ready to give us practical assistance in the field. While all this was being done all the great industries would be engaged preparing supplies for this army when it was ready to go to the front and the Allies, in my humble judgment, would be deprived of a great deal of aid under these circumstances that they are now getting.
We are prepared to do our share; we are all agreed on that. I think that one benefit that will come to the people of Canada out of this great struggle will be the fact that we will leave behind many of the recriminations which have characterized the attitude and utterances of some of us during years gone by. We find that everybody, no matter from what country his [DOT]father came, is a Canadian through and through and ready to do his bit for the *couiitry in which he lives. The war has had a great levelling process in the old land. We, who, in this part of the Empire, in days past have looked with some slight degree of comtempt-perhaps that is too strong a word-on what we call aristocracy of England, are learning that the man of aristocratic descent is standing shoulder to shoulder, and side by side, with Tommy Aitkins in the trenches' and doing his bit as *well as the poorest man who comes from any part of the Empire. We are paying dearly for the lesson we are 'Learning, but behind- the dark clouds there -must be a silver lining, and if each part of the Empire does its duty, as it will, the day cannot be far distant when out of this great struggle will come a clarified, a purified, a more thoroughly united people throughout the entire world, and in this great regeneration Canada herself will have done much and will enjoy the benefit thereof. ,

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question has been very ably and very exhaustively discussed, but there remain a few observations that I desire to make. The question in particular before us is the Budget. There is an old saying that:
Hope springs eternal in the human breast:
Man never is, but always to be, blest.
Last year when we were discussing the Budget we were hoping that before another year would pass a better condition of things would come about. The war cloud is still hanging over us, but we have made fine progress since last we discussed the Budget. We may not be able to put our fingers on the particular advances we have made, but we feel that we are in a much better position to face the enemy today than we were a year ago. We have measured up our own strength, we have mustered our forces, and we have found what we really could do, and what men, money, and munitions we can put behind the mother country in this desperate struggle. That, Sir, is a great advancement. A year ago we were not the organized body that, we are to-day. The great Empire to which we belong had not then found the strength of its various parts, or consolidated its resources. But we have now found the range, we understand the boxing methods of our enemy, and it is only a matter of time and of opportunity until the British Empire and the British people shall give that enemy the upper-cut on the jaw that will put him asleep, and perhaps a little sooner than the Hun expects. We have cleared the seas of the piratical Hun. We are proud to say that on this occasion, as of yore, Britannia rules the waves, and shall continue to do so. Our people have their feet firmly planted on the ground. We have known the worst and have provided for it. We are better organized than when, we commenced the war, and we shall continue until final victory perches on the banner of the Allies. Life is the dearest possession, of man, hut none too dear to be sacrificed on the altar of freedom, security, fidelity, and truth. That, Sir, has been abundantly proven by the Canadian people in their sacrifice of the best lives of the land, and in their sacrifice of money, which is as nothing compared with the sacrifice of the flower of our people. It is not necessary for me to spend any time in going over what has been so well said by many speakers in regard to the stand the Canadian people have taken in .this war. In my observations on the Budget last year I made reference to what was' expected of us by the King, and to what the King himself had declared to be the expectations that he had from the overseas dominions. His Royal Highness the Governor General also declared to us what was expected of the Canadian people, and we are proud to have more than measured up to the highest expectations announced in any of those despatches. Although I cannot entirely approve of the

methods of the Finance Minister and the Government, I am to some extent pleased at the success that has attended their efforts in providing the sinews of war foT the contest in which we are engaged.
The Budget is the real subject with which we have to deal on this occasion, and perhaps it would be well from my Standpoint, as an Opposition member, if I briefly reviewed the financial conditions of the country for a short period before this Government came into power, and very hurriedly from that time down. When Sir Wilfrid Laurier took charge 'of the affairs of this country some years ago, the country was in a very bad financial position, but by his excellent administration, by placing the affairs of the country in the hands of men who understood such matters, men who would exercise economy, and who foresaw the development this country might attain without extravagant use of the means that had been placed at their disposal by the people of this country, Canada was brought into a first-class condition financially. In 1911, when the present Government came into office, the Finance Minister must admit, and did admit, that he found the financial condition of this country to be first-class; he found every obligation fully met and satisfactorily squared up. He found the books balanced, and $40,000,000 of cash available at his hand. The credit of the country was excellent, no bills were falling due, and there was nothing to disturb the equanimity of the Minister of Finance. This happy portion was left to Aim by the Hon. Mr. Fielding, who, for the fifteen years before, had so wisely conducted the finances of the nation. During the very first session after the change of Government, I observed during the course of some remarks in the House that the country had been placed in such a sound	position by	the	wise	andcapable administration of the outgoing Government, that I hoped it would	never again he	found in
the position it was in some fifteen years before. But I reckoned without my host ; I reckoned without having proper knowledge of the spending capacity of the hon. gentlemen who took charge of the administration of this country at that time. I had not counted upon the thousands of hungry hordes that were waiting at the doors, anxious to get their forelegs and whole head into the political trough, and into the treasury of this country. I had not calculated upon the purposes for which the present minister was put at the head of affairs. If

rumor be true, he was put there to provide for a certain class. He was hut one of a number of gentlemen who were returned to power by a certain class wtio were masters of the situation then, masters of the Government then, and who are masters of the Government to-day. In listening to these masters, in giving to Manitoba four or five million dollars to which they had no right; in giving to the Canadian Northern Railway something like sixteen million dollars to which they had no claim; in ladling out dollars by the sixteen millions and twenty millions; it took the Finance Minister but a day, comparatively speaking, to . get rid of the $40,000,000 that he found in the treasury. As the old -saying is, soon he had not a penny to bless himself with.
And he laughs over it.

1 That is the pace at which hon. gentlemen opposite got back to the old stress and stOTm, to the olid condition of things, with not a dollar in the treasury and with the faces being ground ofE -the people by high taxes. That was the position in which the Tory party found themselves, that was the true condition of the Tory party. I suppose that the Finance Minister, having been taken into the Tory family, felt that he must be even worse than the old Tories themselves in order to show that the proselyte was fully converted.
There are only certain conditions of financial circumstances in this country under which our Tory friends know how to rule, and the story which I was going to tell, and which I think I told some time ago, was about a doctor who went one day to see a patient, and discovered that that patient was in a very high fever. The doctor could not make out what really was wrong, and he asked the people of the house to prepare a tub of ice cold water. They got the tub of ice cold water, but when they saw that the doctor was going to take the patient and plunge him into the tub, they tried to prevent him, saying: "That will be the death of him." "Oh, no," said the doctor, "it won't; I cannot make out what is the matter with him now, but I will put him into this tub, and I venture to say that in a few minutes he will develop fits, and I am the devil on fits." The hon. gentleman who, with great credit to himself, now fills the position of Minister of Finance, never really got his bearings until the country was in the old Tory condition of affairs, and then he said: "I see the smoke; I see the points; I know where

I am." With those conditions he started out, and I must say that things have not been much better since he found his bearings, because it was impossible for them to be so.
Last year the Minister of Finance told us that the ordinary and capital expenditure of the country would be $140,000,000, and the war expenditure $50,000,000, a total of $190,000,000, and we had a revenue of $130,000,000, leaving a deficit of $60,000,000. That was the condition in which we found our-selyes on the 31st of March, 1915. For the current year, the minister tells us that he is going to get $170,000,000 out of the people. Let me remind hon. members that, in the old days when the Liberals were in power, and when the gentleman who is now Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) was the financial critic of his party, he used to sit up at night and bewail the conditions of this country on account of the fact that we were collecting from the people from seventy to seventy-five million dollars. Now, Sir, this same gentleman sits back and cheers, as an extraordinary feat of statesmanship, this squeezing out of the same people of $170,000,000, or more than twice the amount that the Liberal Government was collecting. It is another illustration of the "ins and the outs." Of course, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and his friends are now in, and it is perfectly right and proper, in his opinion, that the faces should be ground off the people for $170,000,000, when his heart was bleeding at the thought of $70,000,000 being taken from them in other years. The same cry was abroad when we were spending $87,000,000. The right hon. gentleman who is now the leader of the Government used then to say with emphasis that there was no further nor better evidence required of the extraordinary and unjustifiable extravagance of the late Government than that we were spending eighty-seven or eighty-eight million dollars in keeping up the affairs of this country. Since then there has been a different tune and, a different fiddler, and a first class fiddler for doubling and trebling the expenditure over what it was when we had the reins of power. If the Prime Minister, who was then leader of the Opposition, was sincere and honest in saying that an expenditure of eighty-seven or eighty-eight million dollars was conclusive evidence of dishonesty and extravagance, what does he say as to th.e condition of things that prevails to-day in the Government over which he presides? When we find expenditures of $125,000,000 and $140,000,000 and $145,000,000 within a few years after this Government came into power, with nothing to show for them except the feeding to a great extent of that class of people of whom I spoke before, who have become the camp followers of this unfortunate Administration.
The minister told us last year that in his taxation he expected to provide for - $150,000,000. That, of course, was a guess, and I suppose a minister can do no more than guess under such circumstances. However, when he went to collect the tax from the people he mad,e a fortunate guess to the extent of $20,000,000, which he collected over and above what he had said was necessary. Now, his friends who sit behind him applaud that as a most marvellous feat of statesmanship. In order to get this $170,000,000 that he is collecting for this year the minister had to impose an extraordinary amount of taxation: he had to. levy upon the people an extra duty of seven and a half per cent upon all kinds of goods and commodities that came in free last year, or that were subject to a duty ranging from twenty-five to thirty-five per cent, and an extra duty of five per cent on goods that pame in under the preferential tariff. This is not a light matter to the poorer classes in'' this . country; it bears heavily upon the working classes with small wages, large families, and many requirements, with everything to be bought from the pay received weekly or fortnightly as the case may be. When the minister takes thirty or forty per cent out of the pay envelope of th^Avorkingman he is placing that man in a very awkward position.
The minister was not satisfied with all this taxation, and this year he has come down with further taxation. He comes down with a tax on apples and a tax on oil.. Apples are the luxury of the poor man; oil is the light of the poor man. And now the minister-I suppose unthinkingly, as he has not the experience to make him aware of the difficulties of the poor man's lot-comes down with a policy of added taxation on apples and oil. In jother words, he strikes the apple out of the baby's hand and sends him to bed in the dark. But the hon. minister has indicated that he has experienced some change of heart, and I hope that he will decide to give back the apple to the baby and to re-light the lamp that lights him to bed.
I said a moment ago, and I say it again

with regret, that this Government seems to be to a great extent controlled by the big interests. It was the theory of the National Policy that it would conserve for our own people the trade of this country and that local competition would keep down prices. That was the view expressed by Sir John Macdonald, Sir Leonard Tilley, Sir Charles Tupper and others who agitated for the adoption of the National Policy. They used to say: It is true we put a duty of 30 per cent on boots and shoes, but boots and shoes will be no dearer because the competition within our own borders will prevent an advance in prices. That is a plausible presentation of the case, and the people accepted it, and so the National Policy was adopted. But in those early days we had no knowledge of mergers and combines; these things have developed since that time. But they are with us to-day-the flour trust, the beef trust, the pork trust, the grain trust, the shoe trust-everything is a trust, and with it all we have a trust Government. What is the good of talking of local competition? The people in these industries get together and say: let us not fight each other, but let us combine and we can fleece the poor man. And I was sorry to hear the Minister of Finance the other day, when metaphorically speaking, he threw off his coat and rolled up his sleeves in defence of the millers-the poor millers of this country who are making only fifty or sixty per cent on their capital. The minister feels that he must stand behind these poor orphans, lest something should be done to cheapen flour in this country. But he had nothing to say for - the poor man. In the part of the country that I come from' the labouring man earns from $1.45 to $1.75 a day, and he has to pay $7 to $7.50 a barrel for his flour. On the other hand, the farmer in the West says that he gets hardly anything for his wheat; wheat is so cheap out there that they let it Tot on the ground, for they think it not worth while to carry it to the mill. We have 370,000,000 bushels of wheat in this country this year. There are 8,000,000 people to feed. We have plenty of cheap power to grind the wheat. Will anybody tell me that it is reasonable that the people of the Maritime Provinces, *under these conditions, should pay $7.50 for a barrel of flour? Yet the other day, when the Minister of Finance was asked by an hon. member on this side how it was that the price of flour had gone so high, the answer 
of the Minister of Finance was: " Three years ago we appointed a commission to inquire into such matters, and we expect that in a short time they will'bring down their report." And he might have added: " That report will consist of two or three volumes, and if you want to find your needle in that hay stack, you are welcome to search for it." Is it not most extraordinary that, when such a question is asked, such a reply should be given? I would not have believed it, had not I heard it myself. We have a Government, one of whose members is Minister of Labour, with a large staff, part of whose duties should be to collect such information as this. We have a Minister of Trade and Commerce, with a great Department of Trade and Commerce that might well be engaged in considering matters of this kind. Yet the Minister of Finance, who1 should be the reservoir of all such information, and ready at any time to give it to the House and to the country, was not able to tell us why the poor man's flour has jumped from $4.50 a few years ago to $7.50 to-day. The minister could not answer a plain question, but he could declare his determination to protect the millers' trust regardless of #what became of the poor man. I trust this* condition of affairs will not continue, but that such conditions may be established that when we have an abundance of wheat, or an abundance of any other great staple commodity, the Government will see to it that that commodity gets into the poor man's house at an honest price. I am proud to say that in the province of Nova Scotia, from which I come, though we do not raise a great deal of wheat, our provincial government is endeavouring to meet this problem of the high price of flour. We have two mills built by the provincial government and we will take the wheat from Manitoba and grind it in these government mills, and so will create a competition which will keep prices at a reasonable level. That is what we are doing in Nova Scotia, where we have not the grain that they have in the West, and where we have not the money and the facilities controlled by this Government.
I hope that the time will come when the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce will throw off the shackles with which they are bound and will fell these trusts that they must do an honest business; fell them that, in a country where wheat is abundant and power is cheap, we must have cheap flour.
We have heard a great deal about the

immigration that is to be expected. We hope that, where.as we have room for one hundred million people in this country and have only eight million, the day is not far distant when we shall have a large influx of people into this country who will develop it more and more, in proportion to our means of providing for them. If there is one thing that more than another will make it easy for us to get good people into this country, it is to show that this is a good country in which to live, that this is a good moral country, that it is a country in which children may be brought up in the fear and admonition of the Lord, in which there is a good system of education, absolute freedom for every man to bring up his children in whatsoever^ religion and form of education he wants, and that they will be taught their own language if they want to be without any question or any trouble; that we have abundance of everything necessary for the sustenance of life; that we have no combines and no trusts that can control the necessaries of life and make it hard for the people to live comfortably, and that our Government does not permit or encourage . anything in the nature of combines. But when you tell the poor man in England that a. barrel of flour will cost him fifty cents or sixty cents more in Canada than in London, that is not an argument to induce him to come to this country. I am earnest in pointing out that the best immigrant agency for Canada would be to make Canada a good, comfortable country in which to live, to make the dollar go further than it is going to-day, and to show the poor people that with such wages as they can get they and their families can live in comfort and happiness. I have pointed out that the monied interests of this country have more power and more concessions than they should have, and possibly I need not further enlarge upon that point. I am proud that we provided for the war in 1914 $50,000,000, and last year $100,000,000; and that this year we will provide $250,000,000 without any hesitation. That is, we have now provided about $400,000,000 for the purposes of the war; and I am sure the Canadian people will support any Government in furnishing that money. The regrettable feature is that after this money has been furnished a certain laxity appears to have been permitted to crawl into the administration of the affairs of this Government, so that much of the money does not find its way to the proper spot. We are voting this money for the purpose of buying guns
and munitions and making our soldiers comfortable; in fact of doing everything necessary in order to convert the raw recruit into a first-class soldier and send him to the front to fight with our friends in Europe. It is regrettable to find what a very large percentage of this money has found its way into the pockets of profiteering leeches who have got into the good graces of this Government, which we on this side have no means of preventing. It cannot be denied; it is happening every day. So this money is not producing the fruit it should if properly handled. The minister has the responsibility of collecting this money; let me urge him to see that it is properly expended and expended in such a way that it will bring forth good fruit. This money should be expended with the greatest possible scrupulosity, yet men are permitted to come into this field, where this $400,000,000 is, with no other shibboleth or passport being required than the recommendation of some Borden club or other Tory club in any part of the country. I hope that what has occurred in our political life in the past is sufficient to impress on us that henceforth better conditions must prevail in this country? I am sure that the Minister of Finance would like to see all of this business done in a better way, but he does not seem to have any control over certain factions of the Government of which he is a member.
I was astonished, on re-reading1 the speech of the Minister of Finance, to see the reasoning by which he supported his claim that we have a surplus of $45,000,000 this year. He says that we collected $170,000,000 of money, that our ordinary expenditure was only $125,000,000, and that therefore we have a surplus of $45,000,000.
When the minister started to collect this $170,000,000 what did he say? He said: This is war taxes, we are getting this money on postage, on patent medicines and from the banks; every cent of this extra money we are getting as war taxes and this money is for the war, you are paying it for the war. If you ask any Tory newspaper editor in my part of the country why Sir Thomas White went over to these horrible Yankees for $45,000,000, he will say he went there on account of tho war. Everything you criticise, from Dan to Beersheba, it is nothing but the war. But what does the minister himself tell us about the $45,000,000 he got from the Yankees? He says he paid some of it to strengthen the premier of Nova Scotia in the county-of Halifax and some of it out in the frozen regions of the northern ocean in connection with the

Hudson Bay Railway, and some other works which he would not mention. Not a dollar of it went to the war. That $45,000,000 and the $100,000,000 collected from the Canadian people by the recent loan, was collected, not for the purpose of the war, but for other purposes. Of the loan, one-half - went, correctly enough, to pay a part of our obligations to the Mother Country. I [DOT]care not what the minister may call it, but we are certainly under a huge debt to the Mother Country for expenditures in connection with this war; and if $50,000,000 of the $100,000,000 borrowed from the Canadian people last year went to the credit of the Mother Country, it is not a gift, it is nol given >as an accommodation to them; we owe them at least five times, that much money and we are only paying back a part of our debt. When the minister tells us that we have a surplus of $45,000,000, it is certainly wide of the mark, we have nothing of the kind. How does the account stand? He tells us himself that we paid $158,000,000 on war account .apart from this $50,000,000. We are paying $208,000,000 in connection with the war, and we have a capital and ordinary expenditure of $125,000,000, making a total of $333,000,000. Against that we have the $170,000,000 which we collect, leaving a deficit of $163,000,000. What is the good of juggling with figures and telling the people of this country that there is a surplus of $45,000,000 when, as a matter of fact, taking all expenditures into consideration, there is a shortage of $163,000,000. That is the position in which we stand to-day, and it is a position which was well known to the Minister of Finance when he told this House that we had a surplus of $45,000,000.
I" do not wish to encroach upon the good nature of the House in dealing with this subject. The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has dealt with the new taxation proposals in such an effective manner that I do not propose to waste further time upon them. I am afraid the Minister of Finance will find that the machinery he will have to provide for collecting those taxes will eat up the whole of the money and there will be nothing left.
I am afraid, also, that it will afford the Government another field for displaying their great aptitude for increasing the Civil Service of this country. When they came into office they increased the Civil Service by 12,000 men, which meant an addition of $12,000,000 to the expenditures of this country. Now it would appear

that another field has been opened to the party heeler, and that another bright day is about to dawn for him, when perhaps
12,000	more civil servants, at an expenditure of $12,000,000, will be found by the Minister of Finance. I venture to say that the minister will have to shell out in connection with this new collection of taxes, and, if so, there will be very little left. I fear, indeed, that he will have nothing left, and that he will create another institution like the post office, that will be prolific in producing deficits and in squandering the money of the people.
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance is also going to create new courts. He is going to create a board of arbitration. He is going to furnish machinery by which there will be no end of law suits in the Exchequer Court. I can see here another field opening up to barristers from the Atlantic to the Pacific who will be at the heels of the minister looking for positions. I believe that the officers of the Department of Justice would do this work if they were asked, but they will not be allowed to do it. It would not do to scatter the patronage or pelf among the officers of the department. It must be peddled out to barristers from the Atlantic to the Pacific who will do nothing for it. We had an illustration the other night of what had been done and will be done, in connection with the Justice Department. We had a shocking condition of things revealed. We have a first-class Minister of Justice, a Deputy Minister who is second to none as a lawyer, a first-class Solicitor General, and seven or eight lawyers in the Department of Justice; and yet we had the extraordinary and sorrowful spectacle here the other night of the Minister of Justice explaining that he had had to send to Halifax or to Montreal to get three lawyers to draft some little Bill that had to be submitted to this House.
What did that cost?

Something over $5,-
000. Of course it would have been beneath the dignity of the^ Minister of Justice to do anything of that kind, and the Deputy Minister is not supposed to interfere in matters of patronage, while perhaps it did not come within the purview of the seven or eight lawyers in the department. As for the Solicitor General, he was quite prepared to spend fortnights and months in framing legislation to shut our mouths in this House by means of the closure, but he had

no time or inclination to draft a few lines of a Bill a few months ago.
I would like to make some reference to some of the speeches delivered in this debate. There was a very wild and enthusiastic-I would almost say sarcastic	speech this afternoon from
the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson). I do not propose to pay very much attention to it. It reminded me of the story of the old Scotchman who was sitting by the side of the house on a fine sunny afternoon. His wife, who was a small woman, was most unmercifully beating him about the head and face with her hands. Somebody said: " Why do you allow that [DOT] little woman to throw you about in that way?" and he replied: "Oh, well, it pleases her and it doesn't hurt me." If the delivery of such speeches as that pleases the hon. member for Annapolis it does not hurt us in the slightest degree. He spoke about giving us a portion of his mind in his' own speech. These are things with regard to which he ought to be careful and conservative. Nature did not give him a measure pressed down and running over of that excellent commodity and if he has yet any of it and does not d,esire to part with it I would ask him to put it in his wife's name so that it may not escape him. So far as we are concerned on this side of the House, we will try to get along without robbing him any further of that commodity.
I must give some attention to the veTy excellent speech that was delivered here a few evenings ago by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster). That speech was taken seriously evidently by some of the newspapers of the country. I find an editorial reference to it by a newspaper known as the morning Citizen, of this town, a paper which seems to be well edited, and is held in very great respect in this community. I have not the honour of being acquainted with the editor, but I presume, from his excellent editorials, that he is a man of education, strong common-sense, and good moral qualities. He was moved to say in the Citizen, of February 22:
Looking Facts in the Face.
Sir George Foster's splendidly patriotic address of Thursday night last in the House of Commons will probably remain the outstanding feature of the present session, as it deserves to rank. The address of the Minister of Trade and Commerce serves to remind Canadians that the present Administration contains at least . one really great man-great in the sense that he can divest himself of the habiliments of partyism-
Think of it; this gentleman is going to cut himself out from the habiliments of his party.
-whenever occasion offers and that he possesses the courage of his convictions. It takes political fiber of a quality above the ordinary nowadays to take the attitude which Sir George Foster is apparently ready and willing to assume when called upon.
That is the impression which the Citizen formed of his speech. Now, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said himself, and we will take his own words for it as quoted in this paper:	-
I have been for thirty-four years in public life. I have been a pretty close student of administrations and I cannot point to a single instance in which patronage has helped the status of the bench, the status of the civil service or the public administration or has helped a member of Parliament in reality or a government in reality, but almost always brings the dry rot which breaks up a government. I would wish that in the white heat of this struggle we could speak from the heart and make an agreement between the parties that patronage should have no influence in regard to our public works. If there is any laxity in the public virtue of this country to-day, in 99 cases out of one hundred you can trace it to the baleful effects of political party feeling.
There are other parts of the same speech quoted here, but what I want to refer to is this dry rot which the minister has discovered. It may be remembered that a few years ago he made other discoveries in connection with the election" of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), and I will have occasion to refer to that a little further on.
The speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce deserves more than ordinary attention. The occasion of the conversion and confession of the hon. gentleman should be held as a red letter day in the life and history of the Tory party in Canada. The Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke with the zeal and ardour of Saul of Tarsus after he had been transformed into the new man and had entered upon the new life of Paul the Apostle. It was clear that he was convinced of the iniquity of the practices of his party and of the immediate necessity of the complete abandonment of the life and course of political depravity and corruption, blindly pursued by his party ever since they could distinguish between the right and the left, and that henceforth, whatever others might do for him and his House, he would aspire to higher and better things and, having put his hand to the plough, he would never look back to the Lot possessions of his former days and associations. It is clear that the spirit

of confession and the spirit of penitence were upon him. It is to be hoped that the spirit of perseverance to the end will crown a glorious finality to this notable conversion. As this conversion, at least the confession of it, followed immediately after the able address of the hon. junior member for Halifax, (Mr. A. K. Maclean), he must share some of the honours of this notable incident, and be regarded as the sower who went forth to sow. In this connection we cannot forget the experience and fortunes of a sower of other and more ancient days. The experience of the ancient sower was that some seeds fell by the wayside and the birds picked them up. I could not help fearing a like result the other night as I noticed such birds of ill omen as the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid), the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers), and the hon. Minister of Marine, Fisheries and Naval Affairs (Mr. Hazen), hovering around the head of the earnest and unsuspecting convert. Let us hope, however, that he may break away alive and well from his threatening environment and bring forth fruit meet for repentance.
What are some of the fruits that will be looked for by the Canadian people? First, the Conservative party in which the Minister of Trade and Commerce is such a leading and important factor must be purged of the concubinage of the Nationalist alliance; second, the development of a clean, sound, free public opinion and the expression of it at the ballot box immune from the blasting and damnable influence of the money bags. If the hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce will accomplish these reforms Of and for his party he shall have conferred upon them and his country a boon greater than anything that "science can devise or money can buy." But here let me quote and adopt the language of the immortal Bums:
I backward cast my eyes on prospects drear,
And forward, though I cannot see, I guess and fear.
For we heard some such speeches from the hon. gentleman more than once on former occasions and no corresponding reform, or any reform at all, in the Government to which he then and now belongs. But the hon. gentleman is wise and experienced enough to know that he cannot fool the people all the time and that he has now reached the stage where he must do one of two things-show some fruits of his reform in the life and conduct of the Government of which he is so prominent a factor, or 
come out from among them and separate himself from them and have no further part or lot with the evil works of darkness. Some years ago he feared the inoculation of poison into the veins of the Government and he stated that the electing of the honourable member for South Renfrew would be in fact the absorption into the life blood of the Government of that malignant and deadly element and now he has discovered this condition of the political constitution of the Government has developed into a dry rot permeating the whole fabric with no possible results but annihilation and death. The change of heart of the honourable gentleman in face of the facts as stated by himself cannot but remind us of the belated conversion of the covetous prophet of old who, for filthy lucre, attempted to curse the chosen people of God, and discovering his failure and moral collapse, called out: " Let me die the death of the righteous and let my latter end be like unto theirs." I said at the beginning that Saul of Tarsus had become Paul the Apostle, and indeed the great Paul and Sir George Foster (the Minister of Trade and Commerce) - have many points in common, although differing in sufficient particulars to make them easily distinguishable. Paul was a citizen of no mean city, and in that he has nothing on the Hon. Sir George-as Toronto the Good, the Athens of America, bears more than favourable comparison with the metropolitan home of the aged philosopher, author and preacher of other days. Paul tells us that he was a Pharisee of the Pharisees, and in that role let me emphasize that he will find in the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce a foeman worthy of his steel. Paul says that he was a Hebrew of the Hebrews. Well, if my hon. friend is not a Hebrew, his attainment would justify the presumption, and if a love of the good things of this world characterizes the Hebrew-tell it not in Gath, but it was hinted that the hon. minister was not averse to the accumulation of wealth, impatient of the slow, glacial progress of honest poverty. Paul was a clear-cut, incisive logician, diplomat and scholar; in all those most excellent talents he breaks but even with the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce. But, with all his excellences, Paul had his moments of weakness, and by actual confession we have it that the hon. minister himself is subject to like infirmities. Paul expresses an overwhelming desire to be " freed from

the body of this death." The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce expresses a longing desire to be liberated from a body that bears in its members the disintegrating influences of slow poison and malignant dry rot. Paul tells us that he had to fight with wild beasts at Ephesus, and that he encountered a spiritual wickedness among principalities and powers; in all this, Paul had but light affliction, indeed, compared with the experiences of the minister, for has not the minister attended meetings of the Borden Cabinet, when one-half of that noble band were dismantling and scuttling the Canadian Navy, rending and punching the British flag, and the other half exchanging compliments, 'not of the Sunday-school brand, about Manitoba graft, unclean political records, glue-pot military horses, boots and binoculars. Amid scenes like these it seems I hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce cynically soliloquizing:
How beautiful a thing it is,
And how becoming well,
Together such as brethren are In unity to dwell.
Paul and Sir George, the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, had other mutual experiences, though of perhaps less note. Paul tells us, in penitential mien and tones of self-condemnation, that he was present at the death of St. Stephen and that he held the clothes of the rioters. The Hon. Sir George, Minister of Trade and Commerce, "from his nest beneath the rafters," viewed with calm complacency and approval the slow torture and ultimate decapitation of that venerable nestor of the Tory party, Hon. Sir Mackenzie Bowell. I shall not follow the comparison any further, and hope that the common good in the contrasted characters will deserve and enjoy common rest and felicity "where the wicked cease from troubling and the weary are at rest."
Those are the observations I have to make on the Budget.
